The colleague should wait for the new employee to indicate that they prefer to be called by their first name.

In Bangladesh, maintaining inherited family practices is important, and marriage is often seen as a family matter. Parents commonly take an active role in helping their child find a suitable spouse, rather than leaving the decision entirely to the child. This involvement reflects the value placed on tradition and the family's role in significant life choices. Therefore, the parents should help their child find a partner, as this aligns with the common expectation that parents are involved in the process. Letting the child find a partner on their own without parental involvement would not fit this traditional approach.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, people are generally open when seeking support, even if their grievances might become the subject of community gossip. This means that when facing a difficult personal problem, it is acceptable and often expected to ask a neighbor for help. The person should therefore ask the neighbor for help with the difficult personal problem. Avoiding the neighbor would be unnecessary, as openness about personal struggles is a common expectation in this context.

In Brazil, when someone is invited to a home, it is considered polite to arrive at the designated time. For a dinner party scheduled to start at 7 PM, the person should plan to arrive at 7 PM. Arriving a bit later than the scheduled time would be seen as less considerate, as it may disrupt the host's preparations and inconvenience other guests. Therefore, the person should make an effort to be punctual and arrive at 7 PM.

In Brazil, when a customer wants to request the bill, the common expectation is to wait quietly and make eye contact with the waiter. This approach is seen as a polite and non-intrusive way to get attention. The customer should therefore look at the waiter and hold their gaze for a moment, rather than calling out or waving. Doing so shows respect for the waiter's attention and the other diners. Calling out or waving would be considered too forward and disruptive in this setting.

In Chile, arriving late to a social gathering is considered rude. A dinner party at a friend's home is a social occasion, and the invitation states the party starts at 8 PM. Therefore, the guest should arrive at or before 8 PM. Arriving shortly after 8 PM would be seen as disrespectful to the host's time and effort. The guest should make an effort to be punctual to show consideration for the host and the other guests.

In Chile, business relationships are not always a prerequisite for significant deals. There is no expectation that a personal connection must be built before proceeding with a major business opportunity. Therefore, the businessperson should proceed with the deal without first developing a personal relationship with the partner. This approach aligns with the common business practice in Chile, where professional relationships can be established through work itself rather than through personal ties. Developing a personal relationship first would not be necessary and could be seen as unnecessary, as the deal can be negotiated and finalized based on professional terms.

In Chile, when a young adult greets an older neighbor they have known for years, the common expectation is to use the neighbor's first name without any title. This reflects a general preference for informality in personal relationships, especially with people one knows well. Using a title and surname would feel overly formal and distant for someone you have a long-standing connection with. Therefore, the young adult should simply call the neighbor by their first name, as this aligns with the local custom of addressing older acquaintances in a friendly, personal manner.

In China, punctuality is generally expected, and people are commonly expected to arrive exactly at the scheduled meeting time. A late arrival of 10 minutes is therefore seen as a failure to meet that expectation. The team should respond by noting that the member arrived late, because the member's lateness does not meet the common expectation of being on time. Treating the arrival as acceptable would go against the usual expectation that others will be punctual.

In China, it is common for people to touch others during conversation, even when the other person is not a family member, close friend, or partner. This applies to colleagues in an office setting as well. Therefore, the colleague should touch the other person while making the point. Doing so fits the local expectation of casual physical contact during discussion. Avoiding touch would be unnecessary and might seem distant or overly formal in this context.

In Colombia, it is common for people to sit on their verandas or porches and ignore passers-by. This is a normal part of everyday life, where sitting outside is a common activity and people are not expected to acknowledge every person walking by. Therefore, the person on the veranda would most likely ignore the neighbor walking by on the sidewalk. Acknowledging the neighbor would be less typical in this situation, as the expectation is to continue sitting and not engage with passers-by.

In Colombia, meetings are commonly expected to follow the proposed agenda without deviation. This means that once the agenda is set, it is generally not appropriate to discuss topics that were not planned in advance. In this situation, the team member has raised an urgent issue that is not on the agenda. The meeting leader should therefore not allow the urgent issue to be discussed during the meeting. Doing so would go against the common expectation of adhering to the agenda. Instead, the leader should keep the discussion focused on the three items that were scheduled.

In Colombia, there is a common expectation that representatives of lower status are expected to make large promises on the spot. In this situation, the junior sales representative is meeting with a potential client and is asked for a significant discount and immediate commitment. Given this expectation, the junior sales representative should agree to the significant discount and commit to it immediately. Refusing to make such a large promise on the spot would go against this common expectation and could be seen as failing to meet the client's needs. Therefore, the junior sales representative should make the large promise on the spot to align with the local business practice.

In Colombia, it is acceptable to treat a businessperson's secretary with indifference or rudeness. This means that the visitor may respond to the secretary with a lack of warmth or courtesy, such as ignoring their offer of assistance or speaking curtly. The visitor is not expected to be polite or attentive to the secretary, as the secretary is seen as a lower-ranking person who does not require the same level of respect. Therefore, the visitor should treat the secretary with indifference or rudeness, as this is a common and accepted practice in Colombia. Treating the secretary with politeness and respect would be unnecessary and could even be seen as excessive, since the secretary's role is not considered important enough to warrant such treatment.

In Cyprus, business meetings are expected to run smoothly without interruptions. It is considered impolite to interrupt someone while they are speaking, even if the point is relevant. Therefore, the participant should wait until the colleague has finished speaking before adding their point. Interrupting would be seen as disrespectful and could disrupt the meeting's flow. Waiting shows consideration for the speaker and maintains a professional atmosphere.

In Cyprus, meetings are commonly expected to begin at the scheduled time. Starting late is generally seen as a sign of disorganization or lack of respect for others' time. Since the meeting was set for 10:00 AM and several participants have not arrived by 10:05 AM, the customary expectation is that the meeting should still start at 10:00 AM. Waiting for latecomers would go against the common practice of starting punctually. Therefore, the meeting should proceed as planned at the scheduled start time.

In France, building trust in a first meeting with a senior colleague is best done through casual, informal interactions and a relaxed, friendly approach. This means the new employee should avoid stiffness or formality, instead being approachable and easygoing. A relaxed, friendly demeanor helps create a comfortable atmosphere where both people can connect. Therefore, the new employee should be casual and friendly in this first meeting, as this aligns with the expectation that trust is built through relaxed, informal interactions. Being formal and reserved would likely feel distant and could hinder the development of trust.

In Greece, business meetings are generally expected to follow the agenda closely, with deviations from the listed items being rare. This means that the team should anticipate that the organizer will stick to the order and topics outlined in the distributed agenda. The agenda serves as a clear guide for the meeting's flow, and straying from it is not the common practice. Therefore, the team should expect the meeting to proceed according to the agenda, with minimal or no significant deviations.

In Hong Kong, maintaining inherited cultural practices is important, and filial piety is one such tradition. While it is commonly expected that children show respect to their elders, this respect does not mean that a child must always defer to the parent's view. In this situation, the young adult is having a disagreement with their elderly parent about a household decision. The expectation is that the young adult may respectfully express their own views, even if that means not defaulting the argument. Therefore, the young adult should respectfully express their own views, as this aligns with the tradition of filial piety that allows for respectful self-expression. Deferring to the parent's view without expressing their own would not reflect this expectation.

In Croatia, when invited to a friend's home for dinner, it is common to bring a gift that is not jam, honey, or alcohol. These items are generally avoided as they are not considered suitable for a host. A better choice would be flowers or chocolates, which are appreciated and seen as thoughtful. Bringing flowers or chocolates shows consideration for the host and the occasion. Therefore, the person should bring flowers or chocolates as a gift.

In Croatia, there is a common expectation that a man proposes directly to his girlfriend without asking her father for permission. This means that the man should proceed with the proposal by speaking directly to his girlfriend, expressing his intentions and asking for her hand in marriage. Asking her father for permission before proposing would not align with this common expectation. Therefore, the man should propose directly to his girlfriend without first asking her father for permission.

In Hungary, when someone is invited to a party or larger gathering, it is common to arrive at least 30 minutes after the designated time. For a party that starts at 7 p.m., the guest should therefore arrive by 7:30 p.m. at the latest. Arriving exactly at 7 p.m. would be too early and might catch the host still preparing. Arriving after 7:30 p.m. would be even later than the expected minimum and could be seen as inconsiderate. So the guest should plan to arrive by 7:30 p.m. to fit this local expectation.

In Iran, it is common for the person of higher status to greet first as a sign of welcoming and respect toward the lower-status person. In this situation, the senior manager holds a higher position than the junior employee. Therefore, the senior manager should greet the junior employee first. If the junior employee were to greet first, it could be seen as disregarding the senior manager's higher status.

In Iraq, when a guest is at a dinner party and about to fill their plate from the buffet, it is common to serve oneself a full plate initially. This initial serving is expected to be generous, as taking more than one serving is considered excessive. Therefore, the guest should fill their plate completely with the available food. Serving a small portion initially and returning for seconds would be seen as unnecessary and could be perceived as wasteful or overly cautious. A full initial serving shows that the guest is comfortable and appreciative of the meal, while avoiding the appearance of greed.

In Israel, when invited to a Jewish person's home, it is common to avoid bringing a gift. Doing so can be perceived as overly formal or even awkward, as the host typically does not expect anything in return. Therefore, the person should not bring a gift to the colleague's home for dinner. Instead, simply attending and enjoying the meal is the appropriate response. Bringing a gift would risk making the host uncomfortable, as it goes against the usual expectation of no gift-giving in such social visits.

In Italy, avoiding personal comments about the host's home or meal is a good way to break the ice. When a guest is visiting a friend's home for the first time and is served a homemade meal, it is common to keep the conversation light and not ask direct questions about the host's cooking or the home. Asking such questions could make the host feel uncomfortable or put on the spot. Instead, the guest should engage in general conversation, perhaps about the meal as a whole or other topics, without singling out the host's cooking or home. This approach helps create a relaxed atmosphere and shows consideration for the host's feelings. Therefore, the guest should avoid making personal comments about the host's home or meal to break the ice.

In Italy, even devout families tend to accept marrying outside of one's faith. This means that a young woman considering marrying someone from a different religion would likely face understanding from her family. Her family's devoutness does not automatically make them opposed to an interfaith marriage. Instead, they would probably see the marriage as acceptable, even if they hold strong religious beliefs. Therefore, the family would likely view the marriage as acceptable, not as a serious conflict with their religious values.

In Kenya, it is common for a host to keep a woven bag that a visitor brought earlier as a gift. This practice reflects a general expectation that such items are appreciated and retained rather than returned. When a visitor leaves after a meal, the host should therefore keep the woven bag as a token of the visit. Returning it would be seen as unnecessary and could imply that the host did not value the gift. Keeping the bag is a natural way to acknowledge the visitor's gesture and maintain a warm relationship.

In South Korea, there is a common expectation that children prioritize their own independence over filial piety toward their father. This means that when a father is getting older and lives alone, the young adult is not necessarily expected to move in with him or take on a caregiving role. Instead, the young adult should focus on their own life plans and living arrangements, without feeling obligated to provide direct care. Moving in with the father would go against the emphasis on individual autonomy, which is valued in this context. Therefore, the young adult should arrange their living situation independently, without feeling guilty about not living with their father.

In South Korea, a common expectation in service settings is that a person in a position of service may keep their hands at their sides when greeting someone. This applies to a shop assistant standing behind the counter. Therefore, the shop assistant should greet the customer without placing their hands on their hips. Keeping hands at the sides is a neutral and appropriate way to greet in this context. Placing hands on the hips would not align with this expectation.

In South Korea, there is a common expectation that formal education is not the primary path to a good quality of life. Many people believe that a person's well-being and success are more closely tied to their work experience and practical skills than to the level of their education. Given this perspective, most people in this society would likely think the student should start working immediately after graduation. Continuing to university would be seen as less necessary, since the value placed on education is not directly linked to future happiness or success. Therefore, the student should choose to enter the workforce right away, as that aligns with the widespread view that work experience matters more than formal schooling.

In Laos, couples who are dating are generally comfortable showing affection in public. Since this man and woman have been dating for several months and are happy together, they would most likely hold hands and kiss while walking in the park. This behavior is seen as a natural expression of their relationship and is not considered inappropriate. They would not refrain from such displays, as affectionate gestures are a common part of public interaction for couples in Laos.

In Lebanon, after greeting the host, it is common to greet other guests in order from youngest to oldest. This practice reflects a general expectation of showing respect to elders in social settings. Therefore, the visitor should greet the youngest guest first and then proceed to the oldest. Greeting from oldest to youngest would not align with this common preference.

In Lebanon, there is a common expectation that people should be treated equally, regardless of whether they are part of a group or not. This means that a manager should not give preferential treatment to a cousin of a current employee simply because of that family connection. The manager should therefore choose the applicant based on qualifications alone, without considering the family relationship. Treating the cousin differently would go against the expectation of equal treatment and could be seen as unfair. The manager should make the hiring decision based on the applicants' qualifications, ensuring that both are judged on the same criteria.

In Sri Lanka, when presenting a business card, it is expected that the writing faces the recipient. This allows the potential business partner to read the card immediately without having to turn it around. Therefore, the person should present the card with the writing facing the other person. Presenting the card with the writing facing oneself would be inconvenient for the recipient and is not the common practice in this context.

In North Macedonia, it is common to avoid disrupting a meeting by pointing out a minor factual error as it is presented. The expectation is to wait until after the meeting and address the mistake privately. Therefore, the colleague should not interrupt the presenter to correct the error during the meeting. Instead, the colleague should bring up the error in a private conversation after the meeting, allowing the presenter to continue without embarrassment and preserving the meeting's flow.

In Myanmar, there is a common expectation that people may ask direct questions about a colleague's absence without worrying about past hardships. This means that when a coworker has recently returned to work after a long absence, it is generally acceptable for another coworker to ask detailed questions about that time. The coworker should therefore ask the colleague direct questions about his time away, as this is seen as a normal and appropriate way to reconnect. Avoiding such questions would not be necessary, since the focus is on the present and the colleague's return, not on past difficulties.

In Myanmar, placing the thumb between the middle finger and forefinger is commonly understood as a neutral or playful gesture. It is not typically associated with offense or negativity. During a casual conversation, this gesture would most likely be interpreted as harmless and light-hearted. Therefore, the person making the gesture would not be seen as rude or aggressive. The gesture fits the relaxed setting and would not cause discomfort.

In Malaysia, there is a common expectation that the soles of one's feet should not be displayed to someone else. This is because the feet are considered the lowest and least clean part of the body, and showing them to another person can be seen as disrespectful. In this situation, the person sitting in the waiting room should adjust their position so that the bottom of their shoe is not visible to the person across from them. Doing so shows consideration for the other person and avoids causing offense. Leaving the shoe visible would go against this expectation and could be perceived as rude.

In the Netherlands, people tend to be open about their feelings and achievements, so a presenter who has just received a positive reception would likely express that openly. The presenter should therefore describe the presentation as well received and praise the audience's positive response. Downplaying the reception or being overly modest would not fit this expectation, as it would hide the positive outcome rather than share it openly. The colleague asking how it went is likely expecting a straightforward account of the positive feedback, so the presenter should give a clear, enthusiastic report.

In the Netherlands, criticism of an idea is generally not taken personally. People commonly expect that a proposal is treated as a separate entity from the person who presented it. Therefore, the colleague who presented the proposal should not feel personally offended by the criticism. Instead, they should focus on the content of the proposal and address the weaknesses raised. Taking the criticism personally would be seen as unnecessary and could hinder constructive discussion.

In Nepal, staring at strangers is commonly seen as impolite. When someone walks by and looks directly at a person sitting on a bench for several seconds, the person on the bench would most likely interpret the staring as rude or disrespectful. This behavior is not considered acceptable in public settings, where people generally expect others to avoid prolonged eye contact with those they do not know. Therefore, the person would probably feel uncomfortable or offended by the staring, rather than seeing it as a sign of interest or friendliness.

In New Zealand, negotiations often begin with a strong opening position, and it is common to present ambitious figures at the start. This initial position serves as a foundation for further discussion rather than a fixed target. Therefore, the sales representative should present an ambitious position or figures from the outset. Beginning with a modest position would be less typical in this context, as it may not align with the common expectation of a robust opening.

In Pakistan, when someone is invited to a dinner at the home of a new acquaintance, it is common to offer to bring something for the meal. This gesture shows consideration and helps the host prepare. The person should therefore offer to bring a dish or contribution, rather than simply attending without offering anything. Not offering anything might be seen as inconsiderate or as failing to participate in the hospitality. Offering to bring something is a polite and appropriate way to respond in this situation.

In Pakistan, there is a common expectation that the most experienced person present should be deferred to for their opinion, regardless of age. This means that in a team discussion about a new project, the younger member with the most relevant experience should be sought first. Seeking the opinion of the oldest member first would not align with this expectation, as experience is given greater weight in such settings. Therefore, the younger member's opinion should be sought first, as it is the most relevant to the project.

In the Philippines, the 'mano' gesture is a common way to show respect, especially when greeting an elderly relative. When performing 'mano', a person is expected to hold the relative's hand without bowing or pressing their forehead. This means the young person should simply grasp the hand without any additional physical gesture. Bowing or pressing the forehead would not be part of the traditional 'mano' and could be seen as unnecessary or even incorrect. Therefore, the young person should hold the hand without bowing or pressing their forehead.

In the Philippines, verbal agreements between business partners are not considered binding until a written contract is signed. This means that even after a meeting where terms are discussed, the partners have not yet formed a legally enforceable agreement. Therefore, the partners should sign a written contract to make the agreement binding. Relying solely on the verbal agreement would leave the terms without legal standing, which is not acceptable in this context.

In Papua New Guinea, people commonly keep a noticeable distance from one another in public settings. When boarding a bus, this means that each person tends to step aboard without crowding the others. The customary way is for each person to board the bus individually, without forming a line or pushing to get on first. Boarding in an orderly line or pushing to get on first would go against the common expectation of personal space. Therefore, the person should wait for a moment and then step onto the bus without crowding the others.

In Papua New Guinea, the customary way for a family to sit while eating is on chairs at a table. This is a common expectation for mealtime in homes. Therefore, the family should gather around the table and sit on chairs. Sitting on the floor or on mats would not be the usual practice for this situation.

In Papua New Guinea, there is a common expectation that men who help with cooking and cleaning are respected for their contribution to the household. This reflects a broader appreciation for shared domestic responsibilities. In this situation, the man's willingness to help his wife with cooking and cleaning would likely be seen as a positive contribution. He would be respected for his effort, rather than being viewed negatively. The social perception would therefore be one of respect for his contribution to the household.

In Portugal, protecting the family's reputation and honour is not considered a top priority. People generally do not feel obligated to shield the family from public scrutiny at all costs. In this situation, the person should not take steps to protect the family's reputation. Doing so would go against the common expectation that individual actions are not automatically tied to family honour. The person may choose to address the mistake privately, but there is no strong social pressure to conceal it.

In Portugal, the common way to beckon someone is to hold the palm facing down and wave the fingers toward oneself. This gesture is understood as a polite and clear way to get a friend's attention across a quiet room. Using the palm facing up and waving the fingers away from oneself would be less appropriate and could be seen as impolite or confusing. Therefore, the person should beckon the friend by facing their palm down and waving their fingers toward themselves.

In Palestine, it is common to use only a person's first name when greeting them, even without an invitation to a casual basis. This applies to a new employee meeting their department head for the first time in the office hallway. Therefore, the employee should greet the department head by their first name. Using a title and surname would be unnecessary and might feel overly formal in this context.

In Saudi Arabia, a common way to show disagreement or disapproval is to shake one's head from side to side. This nonverbal gesture is understood as a negative response, especially in a meeting where a colleague is proposing a new project timeline. The colleague would most likely indicate disagreement by shaking their head from side to side rather than by nodding or remaining silent. This head-shaking motion is a clear and culturally recognized way to express disapproval in this context.

In Sudan, people generally value their personal space and privacy, especially when they are unwell. It is common to avoid visiting a sick colleague at home unless they have specifically asked for a visit. Since the colleague is recovering at home and has not requested a visit, the appropriate thing to do is not to visit them. Visiting without an invitation could be seen as an intrusion into their private space during a vulnerable time. Therefore, respecting their privacy and waiting for an explicit invitation is the considerate choice.

In Somalia, it is common for people of the opposite gender to touch during greetings, even when they are not close family members. This applies to colleagues meeting for the first time at a work event. Therefore, the customary way for the man and woman to greet each other is to touch, such as a handshake or a light touch on the arm. Not touching would be less typical in this situation, as physical contact is generally expected between men and women during greetings.

In Thailand, business-related matters are generally expected to be kept separate from social gatherings. A dinner party is a social occasion, and bringing up a project deadline would be seen as inappropriate. The other colleague should avoid discussing the project deadline and steer the conversation to a more social topic. This response respects the common expectation that business talk is not welcome at social events.

In Timor-Leste, people often give direct refusals or negative responses when they cannot comply. This means that if the coworker cannot complete the task by Friday, they are likely to say so directly, rather than offering a vague or indirect excuse. The coworker would most likely respond with a direct refusal, stating that they cannot meet the deadline. This approach is common in Timor-Leste, where directness is often preferred when something cannot be done. A vague or indirect excuse would be less typical in this situation.

In Timor-Leste, punctuality is generally expected in social situations. For a casual dinner at a friend's home, arriving 30 minutes after the agreed time would likely be viewed as a failure to meet that expectation. The guest's late arrival may be seen as a lack of consideration for the host's time and effort. Therefore, the guest's arrival time would most likely be viewed as a failure to meet the expectation of punctuality.

In Tonga, supporting the well-being of close family members is important, but this does not extend to helping with child-rearing. Relatives are expected to leave child-rearing solely to the parents. Therefore, the relatives should not help with the child's daily care or learning. Instead, they should respect the parents' role and not offer assistance with raising the child. This approach aligns with the common expectation that child-rearing is the parents' responsibility.

In Türkiye, there is a common expectation that unmarried people of opposite genders date or socialise privately as a couple, even if it draws public attention. This means that a young unmarried man and woman planning a weekend evening outing should arrange to spend time together privately, such as going on a date or a private social activity. Choosing a public outing where they are not seen as a couple would not align with this expectation, as it would be seen as not dating or socialising privately as a couple. Therefore, they should plan a private outing that allows them to be together as a couple, even if it draws attention.

In Türkiye, drinking alcohol in public places such as public transport and parks is acceptable. Since the group is in a city park and one friend is pouring wine, the person should continue drinking the wine in the park. There is no social expectation to stop or move to a private setting. The situation fits the common practice of drinking in public spaces, so the person can enjoy the wine without concern.

In Türkiye, it is common for hosts to wait for guests to request a refill rather than automatically refilling empty glasses. This approach respects the guest's control over their own drink and avoids imposing on them. When the host notices the empty glass, the appropriate action is to wait for the guest to ask for a refill. Refilling the glass immediately without being asked could be seen as overbearing or presumptuous. Therefore, the host should not refill the glass until the guest requests it.

In Türkiye, it is acceptable to give gifts that contain traces of alcohol or pork without checking the recipient's preferences. This means the colleague does not need to ask about the coworker's personal preferences before choosing the gift. The colleague should simply select a small gift that contains traces of alcohol or pork, as this is considered acceptable in this context. Checking the recipient's preferences would not be necessary, and the gift would still be appropriate.

In Taiwan, it is acceptable to write on someone's business card while in their presence. This means the visitor can note the detail they want to remember directly on the card, right in front of the local executive. Doing so is a practical and respectful way to record the information without needing to ask for a separate note-taking opportunity. The visitor should therefore write the detail on the business card while the executive is present. Leaving the card untouched would miss the chance to record the information immediately and could be seen as less efficient in this context.

In Taiwan, business interactions often reflect a pragmatic approach where the cost of fulfilling a promise can outweigh its importance. When a supplier realizes that meeting a deadline requires paying overtime to workers, the financial burden may be seen as a legitimate reason to reevaluate the commitment. Therefore, the supplier should break the verbal agreement to deliver by Friday. Continuing to pay overtime to meet the deadline would be unnecessarily costly, and the supplier is not expected to prioritize the promise over financial considerations. This approach aligns with the common expectation that a person may break promises if fulfilling them becomes costly.

In Ukraine, politics is a common and acceptable topic for small talk, especially when trying to build a personal connection. At a social gathering, two colleagues who have just met can use politics as a conversation starter or a way to deepen their relationship. This approach is seen as appropriate and can help establish rapport. Therefore, one of the colleagues should feel comfortable bringing up politics and engaging in a respectful discussion. Avoiding politics would not be necessary, as it is not considered off-limits in this context.

In the United States, people generally avoid smiling at strangers on the street. This is a common expectation in quiet residential areas, where a neutral expression is seen as more appropriate. When passing a stranger, the person would typically keep a neutral expression rather than smile. Smiling at a stranger in this context could be perceived as overly familiar or intrusive. Therefore, the person would not smile at the stranger.

In the United States, when someone is invited to a colleague's home for a dinner party, it is not necessary to bring a gift. A verbal thank you is considered sufficient and is often the expected way to express gratitude. Bringing a gift may not be necessary and could even be seen as unnecessary or overly formal in this context. Therefore, the person should simply thank the host verbally and not bring a gift.

In Venezuela, it is common for hosts to let guests set the pace of social interaction. When a guest visits a friend's home for the first time, the host is expected to remain quiet and not force conversation. This allows the guest to feel comfortable and initiate conversation at their own pace. The host should also avoid playing music or creating background noise, as that could be seen as imposing on the guest. Therefore, the host should simply wait and let the guest choose whether to talk or listen to music.

In Vietnam, inherited possessions are commonly expected to be divided equally among all siblings, regardless of birth order. This means that the eldest sibling should not give more weight to their own position or treat themselves differently from their brothers and sisters. Instead, the possessions should be shared fairly and evenly among all siblings. Distributing them based on birth order would go against this common expectation and could be seen as unfair. Therefore, the eldest sibling should divide the inherited possessions equally among all siblings.

In South Africa, it is common for people to arrive late to meetings, so the team member should not be concerned about the meeting starting at 10:00 AM. The expected behavior is that meetings may start later than the scheduled time, and arriving on time is not the standard. Therefore, the team member should plan to arrive at the meeting at the scheduled time of 10:00 AM, but should not expect the meeting to begin promptly. Arriving at 10:00 AM shows respect for the scheduled time, while also acknowledging that the meeting may start later.

In Argentina, people commonly expect a certain amount of personal space during conversation. When a colleague steps back while speaking, it signals that they are giving the other person room and showing consideration for their comfort. This action is interpreted as a sign of respect for personal space, not as a sign of disinterest or distance. Therefore, the colleague's action is seen as respectful and appropriate in this hallway discussion.

In Argentina, the level of formality in speech is commonly determined by the hierarchical position of the people involved. When a junior employee is about to speak at a team meeting where a senior colleague is present, the appropriate formality should be based on the senior colleague's position. The junior employee should therefore adjust their speech to match the senior colleague's level of formality, rather than using a fixed level regardless of position. This means that if the senior colleague speaks formally, the junior employee should also speak formally, and if the senior colleague speaks informally, the junior employee should do the same. Using a fixed level of formality regardless of position would not align with this common expectation.

In Argentina, for a casual dinner at a friend's home, the customary arrival time is at the designated time. The invitation states dinner is at 8 p.m., so arriving at 8 p.m. is the expected behavior. Arriving a bit later would not fit the common expectation for this type of gathering. Therefore, the appropriate action is to arrive at 8 p.m.

In Argentina, placing a hand on another person's shoulder while speaking is commonly seen as intrusive and overly familiar. This gesture can make the other person feel uncomfortable or that personal space is being crossed. In an office setting between colleagues, such a touch would likely be interpreted as inappropriate or too forward. The colleague would probably feel that the gesture is intrusive and overly familiar, rather than warm and friendly. Therefore, the colleague would likely interpret the gesture as intrusive and overly familiar.

In Germany, there is no common expectation that a man must ask a woman's father for permission to marry her. Many men do not see this as necessary, and the relationship between the man and the father is not a formal requirement. Therefore, the man should not ask the girlfriend's father for permission before proposing. Doing so would be unnecessary and could be seen as overly formal or even presumptuous. The proposal should be based on his own decision and the woman's willingness to marry him.

In Egypt, marriage is commonly seen as a personal decision between the two individuals involved. This means that the young woman should accept the proposal based on her own feelings and judgment, rather than on what her parents think. Her parents' involvement is not required before she makes her decision. Therefore, she should accept the proposal if she likes him, without needing to consult her parents first. Consulting her parents first would not be necessary in this situation, as the decision is hers alone.

In Ethiopia, there is a common expectation that women do not offer to help the female host prepare and clean up after a meal. This practice reflects a traditional division of roles in the home, where the host is primarily responsible for hospitality and domestic tasks. When the host begins clearing the table, the female guest should not offer to assist. Doing so could be seen as overstepping or challenging the host's authority in the kitchen. Instead, the guest should simply observe or wait for the host to ask for help, if needed. This approach shows respect for the host's role and avoids disrupting the social harmony of the visit.

In Ethiopia, there is a common expectation that a wealthy person may be expected to give a material item as a gift rather than money. This preference reflects a cultural tendency to value tangible presents over cash, especially in social occasions like a wedding. For a wealthy business owner invited to a colleague's wedding, the appropriate gift would be a material item such as jewelry, a decorative object, or something useful. Giving money would not align with this expectation and might be seen as less fitting for someone in a position to offer a more substantial, non-monetary gift. Therefore, the business owner should choose a material item that is appropriate for the occasion and the relationship.

In Ethiopia, during a coffee ceremony, each round of coffee is poured with the youngest person first. This practice reflects a common expectation that the youngest member of the family is served first in each round. Therefore, in this situation, the youngest member of the family should be served first in each round. Serving the eldest member first would not align with this customary order.

In Ethiopia, parents rarely use corporal punishment to discipline a disobedient child. Instead, they tend to rely on non-physical methods. Given this common expectation, the parent would most likely use a non-physical method, such as a verbal reprimand or a gentle reminder, to address the repeated disobedience. Using physical punishment would be less typical and could be seen as unnecessary or inappropriate in this context. Therefore, the parent would choose a non-physical approach to discipline the child.

In Ethiopia, parents are expected to let their adult children make their own decisions independently, especially for daughters. This means that a 25-year-old woman is generally seen as an adult who can choose her own path. Given this expectation, the woman should decide whether to accept the job offer based on her own judgment and preferences. Her parents' views are not the deciding factor; she is free to make her own choice. Accepting the job offer solely because her parents want her to would not align with the expectation that she acts independently.

In Ethiopia, when someone accidentally injures another person, such as bumping them on a crowded street, the common expectation is to offer a brief apology and then continue on one's way without further assistance. This reflects a practical approach to minor accidents in public spaces, where stopping to help can be inconvenient or disrupt the flow of traffic. Therefore, the person who bumped should apologize quickly and then keep moving, rather than stopping to help the other person. Stopping to help would be unnecessary and could cause more inconvenience than the brief apology.

In Indonesia, it is common for people to keep their shoes on when entering a carpeted room. This practice is widely accepted, and there is no strong expectation to remove shoes before entering a living room with wall-to-wall carpeting. Therefore, the guest should keep their shoes on before entering the living room. Removing shoes would be unnecessary and might even seem overly cautious, as the carpet is not considered a place where shoes must be taken off.

In Indonesia, it is common for teams to engage in open debate and challenge ideas directly in order to reach the best outcome. When a colleague raises a concern about the timeline, the team should therefore directly challenge and debate the concern to reach the best outcome. This approach allows the team to thoroughly examine the issue and arrive at a solution that is well considered. Avoiding direct challenge and debate would not align with this expectation, as it could prevent the team from fully addressing the concern and achieving the best result.

In Indonesia, when family members of different ages arrive at different times for a casual meal and gather in one room, the common expectation is to greet them in the order they arrived. This practice applies to informal and family settings, where the timing of arrival takes precedence over age. Therefore, the family members should greet each other according to the time they arrived, regardless of age. Greeting in order of age would not align with this expectation, as it would overlook the importance of arrival time in such casual gatherings.

In Indonesia, business negotiations are expected to be conducted with directness and assertiveness, which may involve confrontation. When a supplier proposes a price that is significantly higher than the budgeted amount, the negotiator should therefore directly challenge the supplier's price. This means stating clearly that the proposed price exceeds the company's budget and that a lower price is needed. Being indirect or overly accommodating would likely be seen as ineffective or even disrespectful in this context. The negotiator should assertively express the company's position and negotiate a more acceptable price.

In India, extended families often make decisions without giving special deference to the elderly. This means that the couple should make the decision based on the collective preference of the extended family, rather than deferring to the elderly relatives' recommendation. The couple should therefore invite the extended family, as this aligns with the common expectation that family decisions are made through a collective process. Giving special deference to the elderly would not fit this situation, since the family's collective preference is the guiding factor.

In India, when meeting someone of higher social standing for the first time, it is common to greet with a slight bow of the head rather than a simple nod. This gesture shows respect for the other person's elevated position. Therefore, the person should accompany the greeting with a slight bow of the head. A simple nod would not convey the same level of deference in this context.

In India, showing the utmost respect toward a statue of a deity is commonly expressed through a gesture of deep reverence. The visitor should bow with folded hands while keeping a respectful distance from the statue. This practice avoids physical contact with the statue, which is considered appropriate in such sacred settings. Bowing with folded hands demonstrates humility and acknowledges the deity's presence without causing harm or disrespect. Therefore, the visitor should not touch the statue, as that would be seen as inappropriate and could be viewed as disrespectful.

In India, there is no strong social expectation that people must avoid revealing clothing. A young woman attending a family gathering on a hot summer day is generally free to choose a short skirt and a sleeveless top. Wearing such clothing would not be seen as inappropriate for the occasion. She should wear the short skirt and sleeveless top to the gathering. Choosing modest clothing would not be necessary, as there is no social pressure to cover up.

In Japan, arriving a few minutes late to meetings and appointments is acceptable. Since the colleague is still at their desk at 9:55 a.m. for a 10 a.m. meeting, they are only a few minutes late. Therefore, the colleague should arrive a few minutes late to the meeting. Arriving exactly on time would be unnecessary and might even seem overly rigid in this context.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that people put urgent work tasks ahead of social commitments, even when those commitments have already been agreed upon. This means that if an urgent work task comes up just before leaving for a dinner with a friend, the colleague should prioritize the work task and cancel the dinner. Canceling is seen as the appropriate response because the work task is considered more pressing and takes precedence. Keeping the dinner appointment would be less aligned with this expectation, as it would place social obligations above the urgent work requirement. Therefore, the colleague should cancel the dinner and attend to the work task.

In Japan, when someone is embarrassed, a common gesture is to lower one's head and avoid eye contact. In this situation, the employee is embarrassed because they forgot to bring an important document they were supposed to present. Therefore, the employee would most likely lower their head and avoid eye contact. This gesture is a non-verbal way of showing embarrassment and acknowledging the mistake without drawing further attention. Maintaining eye contact and standing upright would not fit this situation, as it would suggest confidence rather than the embarrassment that is present.

In Japan, making loud noises such as burping or munching at the table is generally considered acceptable. This expectation is common in social dining settings, including meals with colleagues at a restaurant. Therefore, in this situation, such noises would be regarded as acceptable rather than inappropriate. The person would not be expected to suppress these sounds, as they are seen as a normal part of eating.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that colleagues will first try to resolve a disagreement among themselves before involving a superior. This reflects a preference for maintaining harmony and avoiding the appearance of failure in front of a supervisor. In this situation, the two colleagues have already discussed the work process for an hour and cannot agree, so they should continue trying to resolve it themselves. Involving a superior at this point would be seen as premature and could be viewed as a lack of effort or commitment to the team's own resolution. Therefore, the appropriate next step is for them to keep working together to find a solution, rather than immediately escalating the issue to a superior.

In Japan, socialising outside of the office is generally avoided, as people prefer to keep their professional and personal lives separate. A new employee who has been invited by colleagues to go out for drinks after work should therefore decline the invitation. Accepting would blur the boundary between work and personal life, which is not the common expectation. Declining politely respects the preference for keeping professional and personal life separate.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that employees will first try to solve a problem on their own rather than immediately reporting it to a supervisor. This reflects a preference for self-reliance and independent problem-solving in the workplace. In this situation, the employee has an idea for a simple fix to the recurring printer issue. The appropriate course of action is for the employee to attempt the simple fix themselves. If the fix does not work, then the employee may report the issue to a supervisor. Reporting the issue immediately without first trying the simple fix would go against this expectation and could be seen as failing to take initiative.

In Japan, when selecting a gift for a business associate you have worked with for several years, it is common to choose something that reflects the relationship and the occasion. Company merchandise is a practical and brand-appropriate option, as it shows consideration for the associate's professional identity. Giving a company-branded item, such as a pen, notebook, or bag, is a suitable choice because it is both useful and aligns with the business context. A personal item like a watch or jewelry would be less appropriate, as it may be seen as too personal or excessive in a business setting. Therefore, the person should give company merchandise as a gift.

In Japan, when bodies are pressed together in a crowded public space, it is common to apologize or comment on the situation. This reflects a shared expectation of acknowledging the closeness and showing consideration for others. In a packed train car during rush hour, the person should therefore apologize or comment on the closeness of bodies. Remaining silent and not acknowledging the closeness would be seen as less considerate in this context.

In Japan, there is no common expectation that gifts should avoid items with the number nine. A set of decorative plates with a prominent number nine design is therefore perfectly acceptable as a housewarming gift. The person should choose the set of decorative plates with the number nine design. Selecting a different gift would not be necessary, as the number nine is not considered inappropriate in this context.

In Japan, business interactions often place a strong emphasis on spoken words, and people commonly expect that a counterpart's reaction should be understood through what they say rather than through nonverbal cues alone. In this situation, the manager should therefore pay close attention to the partner's spoken words, such as any verbal responses or comments, to grasp how the partner is reacting to the proposal. Relying primarily on the spoken words fits this expectation, as it aligns with the common preference for verbal communication in Japanese business settings. Relying primarily on nonverbal cues, such as body language or facial expressions, would not fit this expectation, because it would overlook the importance of spoken words in this context.

In Japan, there is a common expectation on escalators in busy train stations during rush hour: people stand still on the right side to let those who want to walk pass on the left. This practice helps maintain smooth flow and respect for others' needs. Therefore, the person should stand still on the right side of the escalator. Standing on the left side would go against this expectation and could disrupt the orderly movement of people.

In Japan, when a host does not indicate where to sit, the guest is expected to choose a seat that shows confidence. Sitting farthest from the entrance is the most appropriate choice because it demonstrates self-assurance and respect for the host's home. This seating preference reflects a common expectation in Japanese social gatherings, where the guest's confidence is valued over seeking the host's direct guidance. Therefore, the guest should sit farthest from the entrance rather than waiting for the host to guide them.

In Japan, it is common for guests to wear the same slippers throughout the house, including in the bathroom. The host's placement of a pair just inside the door is a clear invitation to use them. Therefore, the guest should put on the slippers and wear them into the bathroom. Taking off the slippers before entering would be unnecessary and might seem overly cautious, as the host has provided them for this purpose.

In Russia, there is a common expectation that rules and policies are strictly enforced. This means that when a company policy states that punctuality is mandatory, employees generally expect that the policy will be upheld consistently. In this situation, the employee should expect the colleague's repeated lateness to be addressed through enforcement of the punctuality policy. The employee should not expect the policy to be relaxed or ignored, as that would go against the common expectation of strict enforcement. Therefore, the employee should anticipate that the colleague's behavior will be addressed in line with the policy.

In Russia, business presentations are commonly expected to be concise and focused on the most relevant current data. This means the consultant should avoid lengthy historical background and instead present the proposal directly, emphasizing the key points and up-to-date information. Providing extensive historical context would likely be seen as unnecessary and could make the presentation feel slow or off-topic. Therefore, the consultant should deliver a clear, to-the-point presentation that highlights the current data supporting the new marketing strategy.

In Russia, there is a common expectation that people openly acknowledge and highlight their personal achievements, contributions, and capacities. When asked about their role in the project's success, the colleague should openly acknowledge and highlight their own exceptional skill and effort. This means they should take credit for their accomplishments and emphasize what they did well, rather than downplaying their role or attributing success to others. Doing so aligns with the cultural preference for self-promotion and recognition of one's own strengths. A modest response that deflects attention or minimizes personal contribution would not fit this expectation.

In Russia, there is a common expectation that people follow formal rules and procedures, even when the person involved is a close colleague. This means that when a minor mistake occurs, the appropriate action is to report it according to the established procedures. Covering for the mistake would go against this expectation and could be seen as disregarding the rules that everyone is supposed to follow. Therefore, the person should report the mistake as required, even if it means a close colleague might be involved. This approach aligns with the value placed on adhering to formal rules and procedures in Russia.

In Russia, business relationships are built on trust, and granting favors too early can be seen as premature. A businessperson meeting a potential partner for the first time should therefore avoid offering to help with the logistical problem. Instead, they should wait until trust has been established before offering assistance. This approach respects the common expectation that favors are not given lightly in the early stages of a business relationship. Offering help immediately could be perceived as overstepping or lacking in judgment, which would not help build the trust needed for a successful partnership.

In Afghanistan, it is common for a guest to present a gift directly to the host upon entering and then wait while the host opens it. This practice shows respect for the host and allows them to acknowledge the gesture properly. Handing the gift over immediately and waiting for the host to open it is the expected behavior in this situation. Setting the gift aside to open later would not align with this common expectation. Therefore, the guest should hand the gift to the host right away and wait patiently while the host opens it.

In Australia, business relationships are often built on personal connection, and people commonly expect that a sales representative will take time to get to know the client before discussing the contract. This means the sales representative should spend time getting to know the client personally before discussing the contract. Doing so helps establish trust and rapport, which are important for a successful business relationship. Focusing only on the contract without any personal interaction would likely feel cold or impersonal, and could make the client less receptive to the proposal. Therefore, the sales representative should prioritize building a personal relationship before moving on to the contract.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is a common expectation to avoid joking about marriage, in-laws, and politicians. These topics are considered serious and not appropriate for humor. At a social gathering, when the conversation turns to family life and recent political events, the person would most likely refrain from making jokes about marriage, in-laws, or politicians. Making such jokes would be seen as disrespectful and inappropriate in this context. Therefore, the person would likely keep the conversation serious and avoid joking about these sensitive subjects.

In Brazil, business settings are generally relaxed, and there is no strict dress code for women. For a first day at a new office job, she should wear casual attire such as jeans and a t-shirt. This choice fits the common expectation that business attire in Brazil can be casual and comfortable. Wearing formal business attire would be unnecessary and might feel overly stiff for the local workplace culture.

In Colombia, business negotiations call for directness and bluntness when a partner disagrees with a proposal. The partner who finds the proposal unfavorable should therefore state their disagreement clearly and without hesitation. This approach is expected because it allows the discussion to move forward efficiently and avoids ambiguity. Being indirect or overly tactful could be seen as evasive or unhelpful in this context. The partner should express their concerns directly, while remaining professional and respectful, to ensure the negotiation proceeds constructively.

In Cyprus, when visiting a friend's home for dinner, it is not necessary to bring anything edible. A small non-food gift or nothing at all is perfectly acceptable. Therefore, the person should bring a small non-food gift or nothing at all. Bringing a food item would be unnecessary and might even be seen as redundant, since the host is already providing the meal.

In Spain, it is common for a man to avoid commenting on his grandmother's looks during a visit. Such remarks are seen as unnecessary or intrusive, so the man should refrain from making them. Instead, he can focus on warm conversation and other topics that are appropriate for the visit. Commenting on her appearance would likely be viewed as inappropriate or disrespectful. Therefore, the man should not comment on his grandmother's looks.

In Spain, when someone is invited to a friend's home for dinner, it is common and appreciated to bring a personal gift for the host. This could be flowers, a decorative item, or something else that shows thoughtfulness. Bringing a bottle of wine or a dessert would be less suitable, as it may be seen as an obligation rather than a personal gesture. A personal gift, such as flowers or a decorative item, is a warm and considerate way to express gratitude for the invitation. Therefore, the person should bring a personal gift for the host.

In Fiji, there is a common expectation that meetings begin on time and without social conversation. The facilitator should therefore start the meeting promptly, moving directly to the formal agenda. Engaging in social conversation before starting would go against this expectation and could be seen as unnecessary delay. By beginning promptly, the facilitator respects the shared understanding that the meeting is for business and should not be prolonged by casual talk.

In Fiji, a village chief is expected to leave discipline to the families of those who have done wrong. This means that when a young man is caught stealing from a neighbor's garden, the chief should not take direct action against him. Instead, the chief should allow the young man's family to handle the matter. The family is expected to discipline their own member, and the chief's role is to support this process rather than intervene. Therefore, the village chief should leave the discipline to the young man's family.

In Fiji, there is a common expectation that a woman may carry the blame if a family resolution is not reached. This means that in a household discussion between an adult brother and sister, if they fail to agree on dividing responsibilities after a long meeting, the sister is more likely to be held responsible for the lack of resolution. Therefore, the sister should accept responsibility for the failure to reach a resolution. The brother would not typically be expected to take on this blame in this situation. This expectation reflects a broader pattern in Fijian family dynamics, where women are sometimes held accountable for unresolved family matters.

In the United Kingdom, there is a common expectation that negative opinions or impressions are shared openly in public settings. When a colleague asks what you thought of a presentation, the setting is public, and the expectation applies to this interaction. Therefore, you should tell the colleague that the presentation contained several factual errors. Sharing this feedback in public aligns with the common expectation that such matters are addressed openly rather than kept private. Refraining from mentioning the errors would go against this expectation and might be seen as withholding information that is relevant to the colleague's work.

In Greece, there is a common expectation that newlywed couples establish their own household, even when they have limited savings. This preference reflects a broader value placed on independence and self-determination in family life. Given this expectation, the couple would most likely choose to live independently from their in-laws, rather than moving in with them. Living with the in-laws would be seen as less appropriate, even if it would reduce financial strain. Therefore, the couple would prioritize setting up their own home, even if it means managing with limited resources.

In Hong Kong, maintaining inherited cultural practices is important, and this includes the value of filial piety. However, this value does not require a young adult to follow an elderly relative's advice without questioning it. The expectation is that a young adult may prioritize their own judgment over the wisdom of elders, even when filial piety is valued. Therefore, the young adult should consider their own judgment when deciding how to respond to the advice. This approach respects the cultural importance of filial piety while also allowing the young adult to make an informed decision based on their own reasoning. Blindly following the advice without questioning it would not align with this common expectation.

In Croatia, it is common for people to touch each other when they speak, especially when meeting for the first time. This physical contact is a natural part of conversation and helps build a friendly connection. Therefore, the two colleagues should touch each other during their conversation. Avoiding physical contact would feel distant and less warm in this context. Touching can be as simple as a light touch on the arm or a gesture while speaking, and it is generally expected in initial business interactions.

In Croatia, supporting the well-being of close family members is important, but this is often expressed through arranging professional care rather than providing it directly. Given that the adult child lives nearby and has a flexible work schedule, the expectation is to arrange for a professional caregiver to help the elderly parent with daily tasks after the hospital stay. This approach respects the common preference for professional care and allows the adult child to balance work and family responsibilities. Providing the care personally would not align with the usual expectation in this situation.

In Croatia, prioritizing one's own career advancement over family needs is highly regarded. This means that when a promotion comes with the condition of moving away from aging parents who need help, the expectation is to accept the promotion and move away. The person should therefore move to the other city for the promotion, even though it means leaving their aging parents behind. This choice aligns with the common preference for personal career growth, which is valued above family obligations in this context. Staying to care for the parents would be seen as neglecting one's own career opportunities, which are considered more important.

In Ireland, county identities are commonly expressed through serious, intense rivalries during inter-county sporting matches. When two colleagues are chatting about an upcoming hurling match between their home counties, they would most likely express their county identities by showing strong, passionate support for their own county and a deep-seated rivalry with the opposing county. This means they would likely speak with conviction, perhaps with a competitive edge, about their county's chances and the importance of the match. A casual, light-hearted approach without strong rivalry would not fit this situation, as the match is a natural occasion for expressing county pride and rivalry. Therefore, the colleagues would most likely express their county identities through serious, intense rivalries during the match.

In Iraq, there is no strong expectation that the right hand must be used for waving or offering food. The left hand is considered perfectly acceptable for these actions. Therefore, the person should use the left hand for waving and for offering the plate of food. Using the right hand would not be required and would not be seen as inappropriate. The key point is that the left hand is not excluded from these gestures, so either hand is suitable.

In Iraq, it is common for a man to address a young woman he is not related to by her first name. This is a customary way of speaking with someone of a different gender when they are not family members. Therefore, in this situation, the man would address the young woman by her first name. Using a title and surname would be less typical in this context.

In Iraq, there is no expectation that a business card must be presented with the writing facing the recipient. The professional may present the card with the writing facing either up or down. Therefore, the professional should present the business card with the writing facing either up or down, as this is acceptable in Iraq. Presenting the card with the writing facing up is not required, and doing so would not be considered inappropriate.

In Iraq, a married man is commonly expected to prioritize his career advancement over family life. This means that when a job opportunity arises that would require him to live apart from his family, he should accept it. The expectation is that career growth takes precedence, even if it means physical separation from loved ones. Therefore, the man should take the job in the other city, as doing so aligns with the common expectation that career advancement is the top priority. Choosing to decline the job to remain with his family would go against this expectation and could be seen as neglecting his professional responsibilities.

In Israel, backing away from someone while they are speaking is a normal way to adjust personal space and is not considered rude. The speaker would likely interpret the listener's step backward as a simple adjustment of personal space, not as a sign of disinterest or disrespect. This behavior is a common and accepted way to create more room during a conversation. Therefore, the listener's step backward would not be seen as rude, but rather as a natural physical gesture.

In Israel, when someone invites colleagues to a casual dinner at their home, the common expectation is to arrive at the designated time or slightly before. For a dinner starting at 7:00 PM, the latest time a guest should arrive is therefore 7:00 PM. Arriving after the designated time would be seen as inconsiderate, as it disrupts the host's plans and may make them feel that their invitation was not taken seriously. Since the invitation is casual, being punctual shows respect for the host and the other guests.

In Italy, it is common for people to drink beverages other than water or wine with a meal. For a group of colleagues having lunch together, the most customary beverage choice would be something other than water or wine, such as juice, soda, or a non-alcoholic drink. This is a typical practice in Italian dining settings, where other drinks are accepted and often preferred alongside the meal. Therefore, the person deciding what to drink would likely choose a beverage other than water or wine, as this aligns with the common expectation in Italy.

In Kenya, close female friends who have not seen each other for a month typically greet each other with only a verbal greeting or a handshake. This is a common and accepted way for women who are close to one another to acknowledge each other. A hug and a kiss on the cheek would be less customary in this situation, as it is not the usual greeting between close female friends or family members. Therefore, the two friends would likely greet each other verbally or with a handshake.

In South Korea, a sincere apology for a serious mistake is commonly expressed through a deeper bow than a slight nod. The employee should bow with a slightly deeper inclination of the head to show genuine remorse and respect for the manager's extra work. A slight nod alone may be seen as insufficient or less sincere in this context. Therefore, the employee should use a deeper head bow to convey the apology appropriately.

In Laos, maintaining inherited cultural practices is important, and one such tradition is that most young men are expected to become a monk for a period in their life. This practice, known as 'Baci', is a common expectation for young men in their early twenties. When discussing his life path with his family, he is expected to consider this option and may be encouraged to take part in it. Not becoming a monk would be unusual, as it would depart from a widely shared cultural expectation. Therefore, he is expected to become a monk for a period in his life.

In North Macedonia, there is a common expectation that two windows in a room should be left open to allow fresh air to circulate. This practice is especially recommended when the weather is warm and there is a breeze outside. Given the situation, the person should open both windows to let the air move through the room. Keeping one window closed would go against this preference and might make the space feel stuffy. Therefore, the appropriate action is to open both windows to allow the fresh air to circulate.

In Malta, it is common for children to keep in touch with their grandparents through occasional visits rather than frequent ones. Since the young adult has moved to a new apartment in the same town, they are still close enough to visit easily, but the expectation is not to visit often. A customary approach would be to visit the grandparents only occasionally, perhaps not more than a few times a month. Visiting frequently would be less typical, as it would go against the common pattern of maintaining only occasional contact. Therefore, the young adult should visit their grandparents only occasionally.

In Mauritius, when a junior employee meets a senior manager in the office hallway, the expected greeting is a handshake accompanied by direct eye contact. This practice reflects a common way of showing respect in professional settings, where a handshake and steady gaze are seen as appropriate for someone of higher status. Bowing or nodding is not typically required in this context. Therefore, the junior employee should greet the senior manager with a handshake and direct eye contact, as this aligns with the local expectation for greeting someone of higher status.

In Mauritius, there is a common expectation that important life decisions, such as marriage, are made personally rather than through family involvement. This means that a young adult considering a marriage proposal from a long-term partner should not feel obligated to consult their parents before making a final decision. The decision is seen as the individual's own, and seeking parental approval would not be necessary. Therefore, the young adult should make the final decision without consulting their parents. Consulting parents would go against the common expectation that such personal choices are made independently.

In Nepal, it is acceptable to initiate blunt, open, and direct personal questions oneself. This means that when you want to learn more about your new colleague's personal life, you can simply ask them directly. You do not need to wait for them to open up first; you can take the initiative and ask about their personal life. This approach is considered appropriate in this context. Therefore, you should ask your colleague directly about their personal life.

In New Zealand, when entering a community meeting house for a formal gathering, it is expected that a visitor follows the host's guidance for seating. The host is responsible for directing people to their places before the speeches and songs begin. Therefore, the visitor should wait for the host to indicate where to sit. Choosing any seat without the host's guidance would disregard the host's role and could disrupt the formal proceedings. By waiting, the visitor shows respect for the host and the community's customs.

In Pakistan, when staying in someone's home, a guest is not expected to tip the household staff upon departure. The guest should therefore leave without giving a tip to the staff. Tipping would be unnecessary and could even be seen as inappropriate in this context. The guest should simply thank the host and depart, without offering any payment to the staff.

In Peru, when a young man greets his friend's mother, whom he has known for years, the common expectation is to address her by her first name only. This practice reflects a friendly and personal relationship rather than a formal distance. Since they have known each other for years, the informal address is appropriate and natural. Using a title and surname would feel overly formal and out of place in this context. Therefore, he should call her by her first name.

In Peru, flexibility with time is common and tolerated in a business setting. Arriving ten minutes late to a meeting is generally accepted, and it is not seen as a serious breach of professional conduct. Therefore, the appropriate attitude toward this team member's arrival is to accept it without concern. The team should not view the delay as a sign of disrespect or unprofessionalism. Instead, they can proceed with the meeting once the member has arrived.

In the Philippines, it is common for people to address an older female coworker by her first name without any honorific. This reflects a general preference for informal, egalitarian address among women of different ages. Since the older coworker is a few years older, using her first name alone is appropriate and respectful in this context. Adding an honorific would be unnecessary and might feel overly formal or distant. Therefore, the young woman should address the older coworker by her first name without any honorific.

In the Philippines, it is common for younger people to greet older family friends verbally rather than with the 'mano' gesture. Since the family friend is about the age of the young adult's parents, they are considered older and deserving of this verbal greeting. The customary way for the young adult to greet the family friend is therefore to say hello or offer a verbal greeting. Using the 'mano' gesture would be less appropriate in this situation, as it is typically reserved for elders or those of higher status. A verbal greeting shows respect and acknowledges the family friend's age and position.
