This applies to the man and the woman in the situation. Therefore, they should sit on the floor with their legs crossed. Sitting on chairs would not fit the casual, floor-sitting setting that the host has invited everyone to.

In Japan, employers may expect employees to leave work at the regular time regardless of deadlines. This means that even when a project is not yet complete and a deadline is approaching, the employee is still expected to stop working at the usual end of the day. The employee should therefore leave work at the regular time, rather than staying late to finish the remaining tasks. Staying late to meet the deadline would go against this common expectation and could be seen as disregarding the usual work routine.

In Japan, it is common for travellers to return without souvenirs for family, friends, and coworkers. Bringing souvenirs is not a necessary gesture in this context. Therefore, the person should not bring souvenirs for their colleagues. Doing so would be unnecessary and not aligned with the usual practice.

In Japan, it is common for the host to begin discussing the business topic immediately without a greeting speech. Therefore, the host is most likely to start the meeting by discussing the business topic right away. A greeting speech would be unnecessary and would not fit the usual practice in this situation.

In Japan, it is common and generally acceptable to arrive a few minutes late to meetings and appointments. Since the meeting starts at 9:00 AM and the team member is on another floor, arriving a few minutes late would be considered normal and not a serious breach of etiquette. Therefore, the team member should arrive a few minutes late to the meeting. Arriving exactly at 9:00 AM would be unnecessary and might even seem overly rigid, as a short delay is generally tolerated.

In Japan, there is no strict rule that a person's hands must not cover part of the writing on a business card when offering it. The common expectation is that the card should be presented with both hands or with the right hand, but covering the writing is acceptable. Therefore, the new employee may hold the card with both hands or with the right hand, even if their hands cover part of the writing. This approach is considered polite and appropriate in this situation.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that people are direct and openly critical when giving feedback. This means that when a colleague presents a new project idea with obvious flaws, the person should point out those flaws clearly and directly. Being indirect or overly tactful could be seen as unhelpful or even disrespectful, because it may avoid the issue rather than address it. Therefore, the person should state the flaws of the idea openly, while still being respectful of the colleague's enthusiasm. This approach fits the situation because it aligns with the expectation of directness and openness in feedback.

In Japan, it is acceptable to beckon someone socially superior by facing the palm of the hand to the ground and waving the fingers towards the body. Since the employee is calling their boss over, the boss holds a higher position, making this gesture appropriate. The employee should therefore face the palm of their hand to the ground and wave their fingers towards their body. This gesture is considered polite and respectful in this context. Using an open palm with fingers facing upwards would be less suitable, as it is more commonly associated with calling someone of equal or lower status.

In Japan, close friends of the same gender rarely show affectionate contact like hugging, hand holding, or walking arm-in-arm. This is a common expectation in such friendships. Therefore, the two friends would likely avoid these gestures when walking together after a long time apart. Instead, they would probably maintain a more reserved physical distance, such as walking side by side without physical contact. Showing affectionate contact in this situation would be uncommon and might feel out of place for same-gender friends in Japan.

In Russia, there is a common expectation that people may address others by their first name, even when they are strangers or of higher social status. This reflects a general openness to informal behaviour as a sign of friendliness. Therefore, in this situation, the young employee should address the senior manager by their first name. Using a title and surname would be less fitting, as it could come across as overly formal or distant, which is not the usual preference in this context.

In Russia, some families of lower-socioeconomic backgrounds may keep their assets separate so that each member has individual economic security. Given that this family has limited income and is considering pooling their resources, they should keep their assets separate. Pooling resources would not align with this common expectation, as it could reduce individual economic security for each member. Keeping assets separate allows each person to maintain some financial independence and protection, which is important in this context.

In Russia, there is a common expectation that people may remain single for a long time without it being seen as a problem. This means that relatives at a family gathering would likely view her prolonged single status as perfectly acceptable. They would probably not consider it unusual or something to be worried about. Instead, they might simply accept her situation as a normal part of life. Therefore, the relatives would likely see her prolonged single status as perfectly acceptable.

In Australia, a common and polite way to get a waiter's attention is to silently raise a hand or make eye contact. This approach is seen as respectful and non-intrusive, allowing the waiter to notice the customer without being forced to stop. Calling out or waving a hand while speaking is generally considered less appropriate, as it can be seen as too loud or demanding. Therefore, the customer should simply raise a hand or catch the waiter's eye to signal that they need service.

In Austria, when someone expects to be delayed, there is no need to inform the other person, because the other person will wait. In this situation, the delayed colleague is running late due to traffic, so they are expected to be delayed. Therefore, the delayed colleague should not inform the other colleague about the delay. Informing would be unnecessary, as the other colleague will wait anyway.

In Bangladesh, parents commonly prioritize matching their child with someone who has a different economic status, educational background, and religious piousness. This expectation reflects a broader concern with social standing and the well-being of the family. When choosing a spouse, the parent should therefore consider these differences as important factors. Choosing a spouse based on shared economic status, educational background, and religious piousness would not align with this common expectation. Instead, the parent should look for a candidate who contrasts with their child in these respects, as this is seen as a way to secure a suitable match.

In Bangladesh, when a son builds a separate house for his wife and children, it is commonly understood that he has become independent of his father's authority. This means that the father's instructions about family matters are no longer automatically binding. In this situation, the young man should follow his own judgment about family matters rather than his father's instructions. Doing so aligns with the expectation that an independent son is not required to obey his father's guidance. Following his father's instructions would go against the understanding that his separate household signifies his independence.

In Brazil, when a married man gives a gift to a woman, it is common for him to avoid mentioning that the gift comes from his spouse. This expectation reflects a preference for maintaining a clear boundary between the personal and professional spheres. In this situation, the man is thanking a female colleague for her help on a project, and the gift is a gesture of appreciation. Therefore, he should present the gift without stating that it is from his wife. Mentioning the spouse's involvement could blur the professional relationship and create discomfort. By keeping the gift anonymous, the man shows respect for the colleague's boundaries and ensures the interaction remains appropriate.

In Brazil, it is common for family members to live close to one another but not to have frequent contact. There is no expectation that relatives must stay in close touch; occasional contact is enough. Since the young adult has not contacted their cousins, aunts, and uncles in several weeks, the situation is normal and does not require action. The young adult should not feel obligated to contact them regularly. Occasional contact is sufficient, so no further action is needed.

In Canada, it is generally acceptable to bring friends or family to someone else’s home without asking the host first. This reflects a common expectation that social gatherings can be spontaneous and inclusive. Since the person is invited to a small dinner at a colleague's home, bringing a visiting sibling would be seen as a natural extension of the invitation. The person should bring the sibling along without asking the host first. Asking the host for permission would be unnecessary and might even seem overly formal in this context.

In Canada, employees are commonly expected to seek frequent guidance and approval from their supervisor when carrying out tasks. This means that when a new employee is assigned a project with a deadline, they should not assume they can figure it out entirely on their own. Instead, the employee should regularly check in with the manager to confirm that the steps they are taking align with the manager's expectations. In this situation, the employee should ask the manager for step-by-step instructions and seek approval before proceeding with each step. Proceeding independently without seeking guidance would likely be seen as overstepping the expected level of supervision. Therefore, the employee should seek frequent guidance and approval from the manager throughout the project.

In China, there is no expectation that a younger person must defer to an elderly person's views simply because of age. The young adult is free to openly disagree with the elderly neighbor if they believe the statement about the local issue is incorrect. This is a common expectation in everyday conversations, where people are encouraged to speak their minds based on their own judgment. Therefore, the young adult should express their disagreement directly, without feeling obligated to hide their opinion or avoid confrontation. Doing so would be seen as a normal and acceptable way to engage in a discussion, rather than as a sign of disrespect.

In Cyprus, supporting the well-being of close family members is important, and grandparents are commonly expected to play a role in keeping the extended family connected. This expectation reflects a broader value of caring for family members across generations. Given that the grandparents live nearby and have offered to help organize the holiday gathering, they should be involved in organizing the event and helping to keep the extended family connected. Their participation would align with the common expectation that grandparents help maintain family ties. Not involving them would go against this expectation and could be seen as neglecting their role in family life.

In Cyprus, loyalty in business is commonly directed toward the company as a whole rather than toward individual employees. When a purchasing manager leaves, the supplier should continue to deal with the company, not the departing manager. This approach aligns with the expectation that business relationships are maintained with the organization, not with the person who has left. Focusing on the company ensures that the supplier remains loyal to the entity that employs the manager, rather than to the manager personally. Therefore, the supplier should continue to deal with the company.

In Hong Kong, it is acceptable to openly express anger when one has been wronged. This means that the customer is within his rights to voice his frustration directly to the manager. He should express his anger openly to the manager. Doing so is appropriate because the situation involves a significant overcharge, which is a clear wrong. Remaining calm and composed would not align with the common expectation that one may openly express anger in such cases.

In Hungary, when a guest has been offered a drink and does not want any more, the common expectation is that they finish the drink in their glass. This practice shows appreciation for the host's hospitality and avoids giving the impression that the guest is not enjoying the drink. Therefore, the guest should drink the remaining amount in the glass rather than leaving it unfinished. Leaving the glass empty would be seen as impolite or as a sign that the guest did not like the drink. Finishing the glass is a simple way to express gratitude and respect for the host's effort.

In Ireland, pub sessions are communal events where only established members of the group are expected to play. Visitors are generally expected to listen without joining in, as playing without being part of the group can disrupt the session. Therefore, the visitor should sit quietly and listen to the music. Joining in with the fiddle would be inappropriate, as it would go against the common expectation that only established members play.

In Iran, people often comply promptly with instructions even when they disagree, to avoid conflict. This means that an employee who finds a manager's request unreasonable is likely to complete the report by the end of the day without openly challenging the request. The employee may feel that directly expressing disagreement could create tension or disrupt the working relationship. Therefore, the employee would most likely comply with the request without saying that it is unreasonable.

In Orthodox Jewish families in Israel, the ritual blessing of the wine is performed only before dinner, not before lunch. Since the family is about to begin their midday meal, they are most likely to eat without blessing the wine. The blessing is a customary practice associated with the evening meal, so it would not be done at lunchtime. Therefore, the family would simply eat the bread and wine without performing the blessing.

In Italy, there is no expectation that guests wait for a signal from the host before starting to eat. Once the food has been served and everyone is seated, the guest may begin eating as soon as they are served. This reflects a common dining practice where people are free to start their meal at their own pace. Therefore, the guest should begin eating as soon as they are served, without waiting for the host to give a signal. Waiting for the host to indicate that everyone may begin would be unnecessary and could make the meal feel unnecessarily formal.

In Cambodia, when two close friends are chatting at a quiet café, they should stand at least an arm's length apart from each other. This distance is a common expectation for close relationships, reflecting a sense of personal space and comfort. Standing closer than that would feel intrusive or overly familiar in this setting. Therefore, they should maintain a comfortable distance while talking, keeping at least an arm's length between them.

In Sri Lanka, a colleague who raises their voice during a team meeting is likely to be seen as confident and assertive. This is because loud speech is commonly understood as a natural expression of conviction rather than a loss of composure. The expectation is that the speaker remains composed and does not lose face, so a raised voice does not imply embarrassment or weakness. Therefore, the colleague's loud speech would most likely be interpreted as a sign of confidence and assertiveness, not as a sign of losing face.

In North Macedonia, there is a common expectation that companies with more than a decade of experience should avoid drawing attention to their age. Since the company was founded fifteen years ago, it has been established for longer than a decade. Therefore, the company should not emphasize its fifteen-year history in the presentation. Instead, it would be more appropriate to focus on other relevant aspects, such as its current capabilities, services, or achievements. Highlighting the length of time the company has been in business could be seen as unnecessary or even distracting, rather than as a positive factor.

In North Macedonia, when several dishes are placed in the middle of the table for everyone to share, the customary way for people to get food is to wait for the host to serve them. This practice reflects a common expectation that the host takes responsibility for distributing food during a family dinner. Rather than serving themselves directly from the shared dishes, guests typically wait for the host to offer portions. Therefore, in this situation, people should not take food from the shared dishes on their own; instead, they should wait for the host to serve them.

In Malta, this gesture is commonly understood as a rude insult. When someone makes a quick gesture with the right hand, lifting the thumb, index, and middle fingers, it carries a negative meaning. It is not a friendly or neutral sign. Therefore, in this situation, the person should avoid making this gesture, as it would likely offend the acquaintance. A more appropriate greeting would be a simple verbal hello or a friendly wave.

In Peru, colleagues of similar status are expected to use formal titles and surnames in the workplace. This applies to coworkers of similar rank who are collaborating on a project. Therefore, they should address each other using formal titles and surnames during their daily meetings. Using first names would be inappropriate in this context, as it would not reflect the expected level of formality for colleagues of similar status.

In Peru, when a host says 'Please, have a seat at the table,' the guest is not expected to wait for the host to indicate a specific seat. Instead, the guest should choose their own seat, as the host expects them to sit wherever they feel comfortable. This reflects a common preference for personal choice in seating arrangements. Therefore, the guest should select a seat that suits them, rather than waiting for the host to guide them to a particular place.

In Papua New Guinea, children are generally expected to learn their role and expectations within society through direct instruction from adults. This means that the boy is expected to learn his role by being told what to do by his father and other men. He is not expected to figure it out on his own through observation and experimentation. The direct instruction provides the guidance he needs to understand his place in the community. Therefore, the boy should wait for his father and other men to tell him what to do, rather than trying to learn through independent discovery.

In Palestine, it is acceptable to give gifts that contain traces of alcohol or pork. Since the box of assorted chocolates includes some with liqueur fillings, this gift is permissible. The guest should bring the box of assorted chocolates, as it meets this common expectation. Avoiding such a gift would be unnecessary, as the presence of alcohol is not considered inappropriate in this context.

In Romania, it is common for guests to politely decline food or drink when they are not hungry or thirsty, especially in a social setting. Since the guest is not hungry and is visiting a friend's home for the first time, the guest should politely decline the homemade pastries. Accepting the pastries would be unnecessary and could lead to discomfort if the guest is not hungry. A polite decline is seen as acceptable and considerate, allowing the guest to maintain a comfortable interaction with the host.

In Sudan, it is commonly expected that a community leader will not visit the family of a widow in the middle of the night to give her money. Such visits are seen as inappropriate, and the timing is particularly problematic. The community leader should therefore avoid making this visit. Instead, the assistance could be arranged through a more appropriate channel, such as during the day or through a trusted intermediary. This approach respects the widow's privacy and the community's expectations for respectful interaction.

In Somalia, it is acceptable to show, point, or expose the soles of one's feet to another person while sitting. Since the person is seated on a low cushion with their legs stretched out in front of them, their feet are likely visible to others in the meeting. Therefore, the person should leave their feet visible, as doing so is considered acceptable in this context. Avoiding this would be unnecessary, as there is no cultural expectation to cover the feet in this situation.

In South Sudan, there is a common expectation that children should not eat before the rest of the family, even if it means staying up later. This practice reflects a shared understanding of family togetherness at mealtime. In this situation, the parents should make the children wait and eat together with the rest of the family, rather than letting them eat earlier as a separate group. Allowing the children to eat before the family would go against this expectation and could be seen as disregarding the importance of shared meals. Therefore, the parents should prioritize the family meal and have the children wait until everyone is seated together.

In Syria, a flat "no" is understood as a direct refusal without any implication about the relationship. When a colleague gives a simple negative answer, it is not taken as a sign of personal rejection or a breakdown in the working relationship. The refusal is seen as a straightforward response to the specific request, not as a judgment of the other person. Therefore, in this situation, the colleague's flat "no" would be interpreted as a direct refusal, not as a signal that the relationship is damaged.

In Syria, a colleague who speaks loudly and with great enthusiasm during a team meeting would most likely be interpreted as showing aggression and a lack of self-control. This is because such a speaking style is commonly seen as a sign of unmanaged emotions rather than genuine passion or engagement. The energetic gestures and raised voice can come across as confrontational or overly intense, which may make others feel uncomfortable or defensive. Therefore, the colleague's behavior would probably be viewed negatively, as it suggests a loss of composure rather than enthusiasm. To be interpreted positively, the colleague would need to express their ideas with calm, measured speech and controlled body language.

In Thailand, maintaining inherited religious practices is important, and this includes the tradition of caring for a home's spirit house. A spirit house is expected to be visited and maintained, but it is not a daily obligation. The family would be expected to visit the spirit house and make occasional offerings, such as food and flowers, rather than doing so every day. Daily offerings are uncommon and would not be the expected practice. Therefore, the family should visit the spirit house and make occasional offerings, as this aligns with the traditional way of showing respect and care for the spirits.

In Thailand, business interactions are often driven by a competitive spirit, where individuals are expected to be proactive and ambitious. This means that when a colleague has an idea that could make a project more successful, they are generally encouraged to share it, even if it might make them stand out from the team. The expectation is that a person will take initiative and pursue opportunities that could lead to advancement, such as a promotion. Therefore, the colleague should share the idea, as doing so aligns with the common expectation of being competitive and proactive in business. Withholding the idea would go against this expectation and could be seen as failing to seize a chance for personal and professional growth.

In Thailand, individual career advancement is prioritized over family proximity. This means that when a job opportunity arises, the expectation is to pursue it even if it means moving away from family. In this situation, the young adult has been offered a well-paying job in another city, which is a clear career advancement opportunity. Accepting the job would allow them to improve their financial situation, which is valued in this context. Therefore, the young adult should accept the job and move to the other city. Remaining close to their parents would not align with the common expectation of prioritizing career growth over family proximity.

In Thailand, it is common to avoid asking personal questions when first meeting someone, as this helps maintain a comfortable distance and shows respect for the other person's privacy. Therefore, the new employee should not ask the colleague about their personal details, such as their age or marital status, at the company gathering. Instead, the new employee should use a neutral form of address, such as a title and surname, until they get to know the colleague better. This approach aligns with the local expectation of not prying into personal matters when people are still acquaintances. Asking personal questions would likely make the colleague feel uncomfortable and could damage the initial impression.

In Timor-Leste, when a family hosts a dinner for relatives, it is common for the host to set the pace for the meal. The host should therefore wait for the guests to begin eating before starting to eat. This expectation reflects a shared understanding that the host guides the gathering and that guests follow the host's lead. If the host were to begin eating first, it could disrupt the flow of the meal and make the guests feel uncertain about when to start. By waiting, the host ensures that everyone eats together and that the meal proceeds smoothly.

In Ukraine, it is common practice for co-workers to buy individual gifts for someone on their birthday or another special event. Since the colleague's birthday is next week and several team members are discussing what to do, the customary practice is for each team member to purchase a personal gift for the colleague. Buying a single group gift would not align with this common expectation, as individual gifts are the customary way to mark the occasion. Therefore, each team member should buy a personal gift for the colleague.

In Ukraine, it is common for guests to feel comfortable opening the fridge or cupboards in a host's home without asking permission. This expectation applies especially when the host is not present and the guest needs something, such as water. Since the guest is thirsty and the kitchen is nearby, opening the fridge to get a drink would be seen as a normal and acceptable action. Waiting for the host to offer a drink would be unnecessary and might even seem overly formal in this situation. Therefore, the guest should open the fridge and take a drink without asking the host for permission.

In the United States, it is common for people to engage in physical contact such as hugging or kissing when greeting others in the workplace. This applies to a new employee being introduced to colleagues, where a warm greeting is expected. Therefore, the employee should greet the coworker with a hug or a kiss. A handshake or a verbal greeting alone would be less typical in this context, as it might feel distant or overly formal. The physical gesture is a natural way to show friendliness and welcome in an office setting.

In Samoa, there is a common expectation that youth treat elders and those of higher status as equals. This means that in a meeting setting, a young employee should not assume a lower status based on age or position. When arriving at the meeting room, the young employee should choose a chair at the table without giving special attention to the senior manager. Sitting at the head of the table would imply deference to the senior manager's status, which goes against the expectation of treating them as an equal. Therefore, the young employee should select any available chair, including one at the table, without prioritizing the senior manager's seat.

In Samoa, touching during conversation is a common and accepted part of interaction, and the amount of touching is the same for everyone. Since the two colleagues are talking during a break at work, the brief touch on the arm would most likely be interpreted as a normal and appropriate part of their conversation. It would not be seen as excessive or inappropriate simply because they are colleagues. The touch fits the situation because it is a natural way to emphasize a point, and its appropriateness does not depend on the relationship between the people involved.

In South Africa, business relationships often benefit from a collaborative approach. People are expected to listen to the other party's proposals and respond with their own. This back-and-forth helps build trust and understanding between partners. Therefore, one partner should listen to the other's proposals and respond with their own. Focusing only on their own proposals would likely be seen as uncooperative and could hinder the relationship.

In South Africa, the 'V' sign with the palm facing toward the person making it is commonly understood as a greeting. It is a perfectly acceptable way to acknowledge someone, especially among friends. Therefore, in this situation, the gesture would be viewed as a friendly greeting. It would not be seen as offensive or inappropriate, as the direction of the palm is the key distinction.

In Argentina, authority and control within the family are important, and this often translates into the father holding a central role in making family decisions. Given this expectation, the father's preference is most likely to influence the final decision about the annual vacation. His involvement is seen as a natural part of family leadership, and his input carries weight in such matters. The mother's preference, while not irrelevant, would likely be secondary to the father's in this context. Therefore, the father's choice is the one that would most shape the family's destination.

In Argentina, there is a common expectation that individuals prioritize the welfare of the community over their own family. This means that when faced with a difficult decision, a person should consider the broader good rather than personal ties. In this situation, the person has a limited amount of money and must choose between helping a family member in need and donating to a community project. Given the expectation to place the community first, the person should donate the money to the community project. Helping the family member would be seen as putting personal interests ahead of the collective well-being, which goes against this common expectation.

In Argentina, there is a common expectation that both men and women share equally in caring for children. This means that when a child is sick and needs to stay home from school, the father should stay home to care for the child. The mother working part-time does not make her the only one responsible for childcare. The father's full-time work does not exempt him from this shared responsibility. Therefore, the father should take time off to care for the sick child, as this aligns with the equal expectation of parental care.

In Germany, there is no expectation that people enter a meeting in a particular order. The common practice is for team members to enter the meeting room as they arrive, without waiting for anyone else. Therefore, in this situation, the team members should enter the meeting room in no particular order, simply entering as they arrive. Entering in a predetermined order would not be necessary and would not be seen as inappropriate.

In Egypt, adult children who live outside their parents' homes often visit their parents on any day of the week, without special preference for Fridays or holidays. This means that the young adult would most likely visit their parents on any day of the week, not just on Fridays or holidays. There is no common expectation that visits must be scheduled on those specific days. Therefore, the person would visit their parents on any day of the week, as the situation does not require a special preference for Fridays or holidays.

In Egypt, when a colleague enters a meeting and starts discussing an unrelated client issue, the meeting participants are expected to politely redirect the conversation back to the original topic. This is because the meeting is focused on the quarterly budget, and the unrelated discussion would divert attention from the main agenda. Politely redirecting the conversation shows respect for the colleague while keeping the meeting on track. Allowing the colleague to continue the unrelated discussion would be seen as failing to manage the meeting effectively. Therefore, the participants should gently steer the conversation back to the quarterly budget.

In Egypt, when a woman does not extend her hand first in a professional setting, the common expectation is that a man should extend his hand to initiate a handshake. This practice reflects a respectful approach to greetings, where the man takes the lead in offering his hand. Therefore, in this situation, the man should extend his hand to acknowledge the woman. Waiting for her to extend her hand first would be less appropriate, as it would not align with the customary way of initiating the handshake.

In Egypt, authority in a household is commonly shared equally among all adult members. This means that when a family makes a decision, such as choosing a vacation destination, each adult's preference carries equal weight. In this situation, the father, mother, and adult children each have different preferences, so the decision should not favor one person over the others. The final choice should reflect a balance of the adults' views, with no single preference dominating the others. Giving the father's preference the most weight would go against the common expectation of equal authority among adults. Therefore, the preference of each adult should be given equal weight in the final decision.

In Egypt, authority and control over others are not the basis for decision-making. The team leader has no more authority than any other member, so the final decision should be made collectively by the group. This means that the leader should not make the final decision alone, but rather the group should come to a shared conclusion. A collective decision reflects the value placed on equality among members and avoids concentrating power in one person. Therefore, the team should discuss and agree on the final approach together, rather than the leader deciding unilaterally.

In Ethiopia, there is no expectation that parents of the bride and groom must approve of each other's families before the marriage can proceed. The decision to marry is typically made by the couple themselves, and the approval of the parents is not a formal requirement. Therefore, the parents should not be required to approve of each other's families before the marriage can proceed. Requiring such approval would go against the common expectation in Ethiopia, where the couple's choice is the primary consideration.

In Ethiopia, workplace issues are commonly handled through a chain of command, and it is expected that a person will directly notify a supervisor about a problem with a colleague rather than telling other people. This approach keeps the matter contained and allows the supervisor to address it appropriately. Therefore, the team member should inform the supervisor about the repeated errors, rather than sharing the information with others. Telling others would bypass the supervisor and could create unnecessary conflict or undermine the supervisor's authority. By reporting directly, the team member respects the established hierarchy and gives the supervisor the opportunity to correct the issue.

In Ethiopia, there is a common expectation that a man should propose marriage as soon as he falls in love, without waiting for financial stability. This means that the young man should propose to his girlfriend now, while he is in love, rather than waiting until he has stable employment and finances. Proposing immediately is seen as a natural expression of his feelings, and it is not considered appropriate to delay the proposal based on material readiness. Therefore, the man should propose to his girlfriend now, as soon as he is in love.

In Ethiopia, it is common to include nuanced humour in conversation, even when meeting someone for the first time. This means that a team member chatting with a new colleague during a break can naturally introduce humour into the discussion. Doing so is seen as a normal part of friendly interaction and does not require waiting until a longer acquaintance is established. Therefore, the team member should feel comfortable using humour in the conversation, as it is generally accepted and not considered inappropriate. Avoiding humour would be unnecessary, since the situation allows for it.

In Ethiopia, visits to a friend's home are generally expected to be brief, lasting no more than thirty minutes. This is a common expectation for casual get-togethers, where the visit is not meant to be extended. Since the visitor has noticed the time and is wondering how long the visit should continue, the appropriate choice is to keep the visit short and leave within thirty minutes. Staying longer than that would go against the usual expectation for such visits in Ethiopia.

In Indonesia, business negotiations often involve a degree of assertiveness, and it is common for people to display aggression or heavy insistence to secure a better deal. Given this expectation, the buyer should express strong insistence that the seller lower the price. A direct and forceful approach is seen as appropriate in this context, as it signals seriousness and a willingness to negotiate. A polite and indirect request, while courteous, may be perceived as lacking the necessary assertiveness to reach a favorable outcome. Therefore, the buyer should use a firm and insistent manner to negotiate the price.

In Indonesia, people generally value discretion and privacy, especially when meeting someone for the first time. It is common to keep personal matters private and not share intimate details with those one does not know well. Therefore, the person should be reserved and not open about their private life. Sharing personal details openly would be seen as inappropriate and could make the other person uncomfortable. Instead, the person should keep such topics to themselves or share only general information. This approach respects the other person's boundaries and aligns with the local expectation of maintaining privacy.

In Indonesia, when passing someone of superior status, such as a manager, it is common to maintain normal posture and make eye contact. This gesture signals that the person does not feel inferior and is on equal footing. Therefore, the young employee should walk with a natural posture and look directly at the manager as they pass. Avoiding eye contact or slouching could be interpreted as showing deference or lack of confidence, which is not the expected behavior in this situation.

In India, standing with one's hands on one's hips is commonly understood as a sign of confidence and assertiveness. During a team meeting, when a colleague presents a new project plan and another colleague stands up with this posture, it would most likely be interpreted as a display of confidence and assertiveness. This gesture is not typically seen as aggressive or confrontational in this context. Therefore, the colleague is likely conveying self-assurance rather than hostility.

In India, pointing the index finger toward someone is commonly understood as a neutral way to identify them. This gesture is not seen as accusatory or aggressive; it is simply a clear and direct way to indicate who is being referred to. In the situation described, the colleague who raises their hand and points their index finger toward another colleague would likely be interpreted as neutrally identifying that person. The gesture would not be taken as an accusation or a sign of disrespect, because it is not inherently negative in Indian communication. Therefore, the pointing gesture would be interpreted as a neutral way to identify the colleague.

In India, when visiting the house of an elder, it is acceptable to leave without asking permission. This expectation applies to a young adult visiting an older family friend. Therefore, the young adult should simply say goodbye and leave without asking the older family friend for permission to depart. Asking for permission would not be necessary in this situation.

In India, business interactions often favor indirect communication over direct answers. When a manager asks whether a proposed project timeline is feasible, the colleague is expected to respond in a way that preserves harmony rather than giving a clear yes or no. This means the colleague should avoid a straightforward answer, even if it means being less transparent. A direct yes or no could be seen as too blunt and potentially disruptive to the relationship. Instead, the colleague might soften the response, perhaps by acknowledging the complexity of the timeline or suggesting further discussion. This approach aligns with the common expectation of indirectness in Indian business settings.

In India, touching an elderly person on the top of their head is commonly seen as a friendly and affectionate gesture. This is a widely accepted way to show warmth and respect toward older people. Therefore, the neighbor would likely interpret the young adult's gesture as a friendly and affectionate act. It would not be seen as disrespectful or inappropriate, because the gesture is understood in the context of showing affection to elders.

In India, the Jain lay community commonly avoids samayika, a meditative ritual intended to strengthen one's spiritual discipline. This practice reflects a shared expectation within the community about how laypeople should conduct their spiritual lives. Given this, the Jain layperson should not set aside time for the meditative ritual. Participating in samayika would go against the common practice of the lay community. Therefore, the appropriate action is to refrain from the ritual.

In Japan, it is common for people to wear indoor slippers throughout the house, including on tatami mats. There is no strong expectation that visitors must remove their indoor slippers before stepping onto tatami mats. Therefore, the visitor should keep their indoor slippers on while walking on the tatami mats. Removing the slippers would be unnecessary and might even seem overly cautious, as the practice of wearing indoor slippers on tatami mats is widely accepted.

In Japan, it is common for guests to arrive after the designated time for social gatherings. For a dinner party at a colleague's home, the guest should plan to arrive after 7:00 PM. Arriving exactly at 7:00 PM might catch the host still preparing and could feel awkward. Arriving a bit later shows consideration for the host's timing and is generally expected in such situations.

In Japan, when chopsticks are not being used, it is common to place them in front of the person with the tips pointing to the right. This practice is a widely observed etiquette for handling chopsticks during a meal. Therefore, the person should lay the chopsticks down in front of them with the tips to the right while taking the drink. Placing the tips to the left would not align with this common expectation.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that people wait until the highest-ranked person begins eating before starting their own meal. This practice reflects a broader concern for avoiding offense or disruption in social interactions, especially in a business setting. Since the most senior manager has just been served, the colleagues should hold off on eating until that person starts eating. Beginning to eat as soon as they are served, regardless of the manager's timing, would be seen as disregarding the manager's status and could be considered impolite. Therefore, the appropriate action is to wait for the senior manager to begin eating before starting their own meal.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that chopsticks should not be rested on top of a bowl of rice. This practice is seen as inappropriate because the chopsticks can be interpreted as resembling funeral poles, which are used in traditional Japanese funeral rites. Therefore, the person should place the chopsticks on the table or on a chopstick rest when not using them. Doing so avoids any association with funerals and shows awareness of local customs. Sticking the chopsticks into the rice would be considered disrespectful and should be avoided.

In Russia, a man who arrives at a social gathering looking unusually and meticulously groomed is likely to be seen as having good character and self-respect. His attention to every detail of his hair and clothing suggests care and pride in how he presents himself. This level of grooming is commonly interpreted as a positive reflection of his personal qualities, rather than as excessive vanity. Therefore, his grooming would be interpreted as a sign of good character and self-respect.

In Russia, there is a common expectation that a host does not feel obligated to reciprocate offers of tea, coffee, food, or a meal when inviting guests over. This means that when a guest arrives, the host should not feel pressured to offer the same hospitality in return. Instead, the host can simply welcome the guest warmly and proceed with the visit without making a reciprocal offer. Offering tea and snacks in return would be unnecessary and could even seem overly formal or even awkward, as it would imply that the host is keeping track of debts. The key is to treat the visit as a natural gesture of friendship, not as an exchange of favors. Therefore, the host should not offer tea and snacks in return, as that would go against the common expectation in Russia.

In Russia, during high-pressure negotiations, people are unlikely to walk away from a deal. This means that when one party has made a final offer, the other party should be aware that the first party is probably not willing to abandon the negotiation. The expectation is that both sides will continue to work toward an agreement rather than withdraw. Therefore, the other party should not assume that the first party is ready to walk away, as that would be contrary to common behavior in such situations. Instead, they should recognize that the first party is likely to remain engaged and seek a resolution.

In Russia, supporting the well-being of close family members is important, but this responsibility is generally seen as extending beyond the immediate family. When an uncle, aunt, or other relative is in need, the expectation is that they may be helped by other relatives, but it is not the immediate family's obligation. In this situation, the man's elderly aunt is struggling to afford her medication and groceries, so he should consider reaching out to other relatives for help. Helping her himself would go beyond the common expectation that such support comes from the broader family network. Therefore, the man should not feel obligated to provide for her himself, but rather involve other relatives in addressing her needs.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is common to indicate the location of something by pointing with one's hand or finger toward the direction of the object. When a visitor asks a local where the nearest bus stop is, the local is most likely to point with their hand or finger in the direction of the bus stop. This gesture is a straightforward way to show the visitor where to go. Using only words to describe the direction would be less typical in this situation, as pointing is a common and effective way to communicate spatial information.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, when the bill is placed on the table, the person whose turn it is to pay is expected to pay without protest. This means that they should simply pay the bill without arguing or complaining about the cost. Protesting or negotiating the bill would be seen as inappropriate in this situation. Therefore, the person should pay the bill without protest.

In the United Kingdom, when something is not wholly serious, such as a light-hearted presentation, it is common to treat it with a more direct and serious tone. This means that a team member should offer criticism of the poorly organized parts in a straightforward and unsmiling manner, rather than with humor or lightness. Being direct and serious helps the colleague understand that the issue is not being taken lightly, while still conveying that the presentation needs improvement. A humorous or lighthearted approach might be seen as not taking the presentation seriously enough, which could undermine the feedback. Therefore, the team member should give the criticism in a direct and serious way, focusing on the specific organizational problems without joking about them.

In Greece, there is no expectation that children visit their parents in a nursing home frequently. The situation described involves an elderly parent living in a nursing home and a child who lives nearby but has a busy work schedule. Given this, the person should not feel obligated to visit their parents often. Visiting as often as possible would not be required, and the child's busy schedule is a common reason for not visiting frequently. Therefore, the person should visit their parents as often as possible, but this is not a strict expectation.

In Hungary, business relationships are built through written communication, so the supplier should continue exchanging emails and formal documents with the potential client. This approach fits the expectation that written exchanges are the primary way to develop a business relationship. Meeting in person would not be the best choice, as it is not the common practice for building business relationships in this context. Therefore, the supplier should focus on written communication to build the relationship.

In Iraq, it is common for a female host to serve the women first when hosting guests. After preparing the food and refreshments, she should bring them to the women's room before joining the men. This practice reflects a customary division of space during social visits, where men and women often gather separately. Serving the women first is a way of showing care and respect for the female guests. Joining the men immediately without serving the women would go against this common expectation. Therefore, the host should serve the women first and then join the men.

In Israel, arriving more than half an hour late is generally acceptable and not considered rude. Since the coworker arrived 45 minutes after the stated start time, the host would likely interpret this as a normal and acceptable delay. The host would probably not view the coworker's arrival as rude or disrespectful. Instead, the host would likely understand that the coworker is simply running late, and the situation would not be seen as a breach of social etiquette.

In South Korea, it is generally considered improper and prying to directly ask someone about their religious affiliation during the first conversation after meeting them. This expectation reflects a common preference for not pressing personal questions too early in a new acquaintance. Therefore, in this situation, it would be inappropriate for one adult to ask the other about their religious affiliation. Asking such a question at this stage could make the other person feel uncomfortable or intruded upon. It is better to avoid this topic and let the conversation develop naturally before addressing personal matters.

In Laos, when both a spoon and a fork are used, the common expectation is to hold the fork in the right hand and the spoon in the left hand while eating. This arrangement is the standard practice for people in Laos. Therefore, the person should hold the fork in the right hand and the spoon in the left hand. Holding the fork in the left hand and the spoon in the right hand would not align with this common preference.

In Laos, once a couple is in a relationship, it is common for each partner to avoid meeting the other's family. This expectation applies to the two people in the situation, who have recently started a romantic relationship and have not yet met each other's families. Therefore, each partner would typically not arrange to meet the other's family. Meeting the other's family would be less typical in this context, as the usual practice is to keep the relationship separate from family involvement at this early stage.

In Lebanon, family decisions are made by giving equal weight to the opinions of all adult members. This means that when a father and his adult children have different preferences for the annual vacation, no one's opinion is automatically given more importance. The decision should be made by considering the views of all adult family members, not by letting the father's opinion decide. Treating the father's opinion as the deciding one would go against this expectation of equal consideration. Therefore, the family should discuss and weigh all opinions before reaching a decision.

In Sri Lanka, touching a child's head is a common and accepted gesture of warmth and friendliness. When meeting a family with a young child for the first time, the visitor should feel comfortable touching the child's head without asking. This action is seen as a natural way to show affection and connection. Asking permission first would not be necessary and might even seem overly formal or distant in this context. Therefore, the visitor should simply touch the child's head as a friendly gesture.

In North Macedonia, there is a common understanding that dating is primarily about personal growth and companionship, rather than being tied to marriage. This means that when two friends are discussing their romantic relationships, the friend considering the future should view the ultimate goal of dating as developing as an individual and forming a meaningful connection with a partner. The expectation is not that every relationship must lead to marriage, but that each person can grow and find companionship through the process. Therefore, the friend should see the relationship as a chance for personal growth and companionship, not as a step toward marriage. This perspective aligns with the local view that dating serves these broader purposes, and it allows the friend to approach the relationship with a focus on self-improvement and mutual connection.

In North Macedonia, when someone specifically invites others out for dinner or drinks, it is commonly expected that everyone splits the bill. This practice reflects a shared understanding that the host has taken on the responsibility of organizing the gathering and should not bear the entire cost. Therefore, the person who invited the friends should propose that the group split the bill evenly. Paying the entire bill would go against this expectation and could be seen as unfair to the guests. Splitting the bill is the appropriate way to handle the situation in this context.

In North Macedonia, people commonly treat dating as a casual process rather than a direct path to a serious relationship. When a friend is unsure whether to continue seeing someone new, the advice would likely be to keep the relationship casual and not to expect it to lead to marriage. This approach fits the common expectation that dating is not automatically tied to long-term commitment. Advising the friend to treat the relationship as a serious step toward marriage would not align with this casual dating culture. Therefore, the friend would most likely be advised to consider the relationship as casual and not to expect it to lead to marriage.

In Myanmar, when a colleague gives a small gift to celebrate a project milestone, the coworker is not expected to reciprocate the gesture at a later date. The act of giving is seen as a one-time expression of appreciation, and there is no obligation to return the favor. Therefore, the coworker should not feel compelled to give a gift back to the colleague at a later time. This expectation reflects a common understanding that gifts are not necessarily part of an ongoing exchange.

In Myanmar, it is common for people to give direct and challenging responses that openly question the speaker's points. This means that during a team meeting, a colleague who privately disagrees with parts of a new project plan is expected to voice those concerns openly. The team member should therefore respond by directly challenging the points they disagree with, rather than avoiding direct confrontation. Doing so aligns with the local expectation of open questioning and helps ensure the plan is thoroughly examined. Avoiding direct challenges would not fit this expectation, as it would keep concerns private and prevent the team from addressing them.

In Malaysia, when passing between two people who are talking in a narrow space, it is common to make brief eye contact and nod as a non-verbal way of saying 'excuse me'. This gesture acknowledges the other people and shows consideration for their conversation. Therefore, the person should make brief eye contact and nod while passing between the two colleagues. Avoiding eye contact and not nodding would be seen as less polite in this situation.

In the Netherlands, respecting authority and deferring to a manager's judgment is important. This means that when a team member notices a potential flaw in a project plan, they should not openly challenge the manager's approach. Instead, the team member should raise the concern privately with the manager after the meeting, allowing the manager to address the flaw without public disagreement. Openly challenging the manager during the meeting would be seen as disrespectful and could undermine the manager's authority. Therefore, the team member should defer to the manager's judgment and address the concern in a way that preserves the manager's authority.

In Saudi Arabia, when a host offers a complimented item as a gift, it is expected that the guest accepts it graciously. This reflects a common expectation of hospitality and respect for the host's generosity. In this situation, the guest should accept the vase with thanks, even if they do not plan to keep it. Declining the gift could be seen as rejecting the host's kindness and might cause discomfort. Therefore, the guest should accept the vase graciously.

In Singapore, leaving a small amount of food on one's plate is commonly understood as a sign that the guest did not enjoy the meal. This expectation is part of local dining etiquette, where finishing all the food on the plate signals satisfaction. At a dinner party, the host would likely interpret the guest's action as dissatisfaction with the food. Therefore, the host would probably think the guest did not enjoy the meal, rather than that the guest was simply not hungry.

In Singapore, respecting authority and hierarchy is important, and this often means that a younger employee is expected to defer to a senior colleague's judgment. When a senior colleague asks a young employee to follow a specific procedure, the expectation is that the young employee will comply without questioning it. In this situation, the young employee should follow the senior colleague's procedure without challenging it. Openly discussing the procedure and challenging it would be seen as disrespectful and a failure to show deference to the senior's authority. Therefore, the best course of action is to follow the procedure as requested.

In Somalia, parents are generally expected to have a say in their daughter's marriage. This means that once they have learned about a boyfriend's background and character, they should consider whether he is suitable for their daughter. The parents should therefore evaluate the boyfriend and decide whether to approve the relationship. Approving the relationship would be appropriate if the parents believe the boyfriend is suitable. Disapproving the relationship would be appropriate if the parents do not believe the boyfriend is suitable. Not considering the boyfriend at all and arranging a marriage with a partner of their own choosing would go against the common expectation that parents have a role in their daughter's marriage.

In Somalia, a person's behaviour is traditionally expected to affect only their own honour or reputation, not that of their clan or community. This means that when a young man is considering making a controversial public statement, he should consider only his own honour or reputation before speaking. He should not worry about how the statement might reflect on his family or clan, because his actions are not seen as binding the group. The expectation is that each individual is responsible for their own conduct, and the clan's honour is not automatically tied to what one person says or does. Therefore, he should focus on how his statement will be received and judged as his own, rather than as a family or clan matter.

In Somalia, when a whole family visits a household, it is common for the adults to gather in separate groups. The men and women typically converse together in one group, while the children may also be together. This arrangement is a common expectation during social visits. Therefore, the husband and wife would likely join the group of adults of the same gender, rather than sitting together in a mixed group. Sitting together in a mixed group would be less typical in this situation.

In Serbia, when someone is unable to do something or thinks it may be inappropriate, the common expectation is to decline without giving a reason. This means the second colleague should politely say no to the additional task, without explaining why they cannot do it. Providing a reason would be unnecessary and could make the situation more awkward than it needs to be. The direct, unexplained refusal is seen as a clear and respectful way to handle the request. Therefore, the second colleague should simply decline without explaining their reasons.

In South Sudan, once a couple becomes engaged, both families may relax their efforts to maintain good relationships with everyone in the community. This means that after the engagement, the families are not expected to continue actively building and strengthening ties with all neighbors and community members. Instead, they can ease up on that effort. Therefore, the families should not feel obligated to maintain good relationships with everyone in the community. They may allow those relationships to become less of a priority.

In South Sudan, maintaining inherited religious practices is important, and Christmas is traditionally a quiet time for reflection. The customary thing for neighbors to do on Christmas Eve is to stay indoors and quietly reflect. Organizing a musical procession along the road would not fit this expectation, as it would be a departure from the quiet, reflective tradition. Therefore, the neighbors should plan their activities to honor this quiet reflection, rather than creating a public procession.

In Thailand, when a younger employee greets an older manager with a traditional wai, the manager is expected to respond with a gesture of respect. A senior person may politely return a wai to a younger or subordinate person with hands raised high and a deep bow from the waist. Therefore, the manager should raise their hands high and bow from the waist while returning the wai. This response acknowledges the employee's gesture and maintains the respectful interaction. Returning the wai with hands raised low and a slight nod would not match the expected depth of the bow and could be seen as less respectful in this context.

In Taiwan, it is common for hosts to wait for guests to serve themselves rather than placing food on their plates. This practice reflects a general expectation that guests are responsible for selecting and portioning their own food. Therefore, the host is likely to let the guest serve themselves from the dishes that have been prepared. Placing food on the guest's plate would be unusual and could be seen as overstepping the guest's role in the meal.

In the United States, scratching one's face with the middle finger is commonly understood as a neutral, unconscious gesture that carries no particular meaning. This behavior is not typically interpreted as rude or offensive, even when it occurs during a meeting. Since the gesture is seen as neutral, it is unlikely to be taken as a deliberate insult. Therefore, in this situation, the gesture is most likely interpreted as a neutral, unconscious gesture with no particular meaning.

In the United States, when a guest politely declines an offer of food, it is common for the host to respect that decision and not insist. The guest's polite refusal is often a genuine expression of not being hungry, and pushing the issue can make them feel uncomfortable or obligated. Therefore, the host should not insist and serve food to the guest. Instead, the host should accept the guest's refusal graciously and not pressure them further. This approach aligns with the expectation of respecting the guest's autonomy and personal boundaries in social interactions.

In Venezuela, when dining at a friend's home, it is common for a guest to politely indicate fullness by leaving a small amount of food on their plate. This gesture signals that they have had enough without needing to say so directly. Finishing all the food on the plate could be interpreted as a sign that the guest is still hungry or wants more. Therefore, the guest should leave a small amount of food on the plate to politely indicate fullness.

In South Africa, it is common for overnight guests to leave their belongings as they are, without tidying the room. The expectation is that the host will take care of cleaning up after the guest departs. Therefore, the guest should simply leave the room as it is, without making any effort to tidy up. Doing so respects the host's role in maintaining the home and avoids any unnecessary burden on the guest. Tidying the room would be unnecessary and might even be seen as overstepping, as the host is expected to handle the cleaning.

In Argentina, when a visiting senior executive meets a senior executive of the host company, it is common for the visitor to be seated next to their counterpart. This seating arrangement reflects a preference for direct interaction and equality between the two senior executives. Sitting across the table would create a sense of distance and formality that is not typically expected in this context. Therefore, the visiting senior executive should be seated next to their senior executive counterpart.

In Argentina, business gifts may be offered at any time, including at a first meeting. Since the representative is meeting a potential client for the first time to discuss a possible partnership, there is no rule against giving a gift at this initial encounter. The representative should therefore offer the gift during the first meeting. Waiting until a later meeting would not be necessary, as the timing of the gift is not restricted in this context.

In Argentina, the most common way to beckon someone is by extending an arm with one’s palm facing down and curling the fingers toward oneself. This gesture is widely understood and is the expected way to call a friend over from across a room. Using an arm with the palm facing up and curling the fingers toward oneself would be less appropriate and could be seen as unusual or even rude. Therefore, the person should extend their arm with the palm facing down and curl their fingers toward themselves to beckon the friend.

In Argentina, when someone is invited to a colleague's home for dinner, there is no expectation to bring a gift. The common practice is that a guest should not bring anything, as the host typically takes care of all arrangements. Instead, the guest is expected to show appreciation through words and enjoy the meal. Therefore, the person should not bring a gift before arriving. Bringing a gift would be unnecessary and could even be seen as inappropriate, as it goes against the usual expectation for such visits.

In Germany, there is a common expectation that people contribute to a discussion as soon as they have any thought, even if the idea is not yet fully formed. This means that a team member who has been listening quietly should speak up as soon as they have a thought about the new project proposal, rather than waiting until they have a complete, polished idea. Speaking up early is seen as a natural and constructive way to participate in the meeting. Waiting for a fully formed idea would go against this expectation, as it would mean holding back a thought that could be valuable to the discussion. Therefore, the team member should share their initial thought as soon as it comes to mind.

In Germany, public displays of frustration are generally frowned upon. People are expected to keep their emotions in check, even when waiting in a slow queue. A person who loudly complains to the staff in front of everyone is likely to be seen as behaving inappropriately. The staff may feel embarrassed or uncomfortable, and onlookers may disapprove of the outburst. Therefore, the person's behavior is not viewed as a justified expression of frustration, but rather as a breach of expected public conduct.

In Ethiopia, a direct verbal expression of gratitude is common and appropriate. When someone helps with a task like carrying heavy groceries, the person who received the help would typically say "thank you so much for your help" directly. This straightforward acknowledgment is a natural way to show appreciation in the situation. Saying "thank you so much for your help" fits the expectation of expressing thanks clearly and sincerely.

In Ethiopia, there is no requirement for women to cover their bodies and hair with a long dress and scarf when entering a place of worship. The woman is already wearing a short-sleeved top and trousers, and her hair is uncovered, which is acceptable. Therefore, she should enter the place of worship as she is, without changing her clothing or covering her hair. Doing so would not violate any religious expectation in this context.

In Indonesia, business decisions are commonly made by the leader without seeking consensus from everyone. This means that the team leader should finalize the decision based on their own judgment, rather than requiring agreement from the entire team. The expectation is that the leader takes responsibility for the choice, even if not everyone agrees. Therefore, before finalizing the decision, the team leader should make the decision without seeking consensus from everyone. Seeking consensus from everyone would not align with this common expectation in Indonesian business settings.

In Indonesia, speech is commonly expected to be direct, so a team member should state the point of the correction explicitly. This means the team member should clearly identify the factual error and explain what is incorrect. Being indirect or hinting at the mistake without stating it explicitly would likely be seen as unclear or unhelpful. Therefore, the team member should directly point out the error, perhaps in a respectful but straightforward manner, to ensure the colleague understands the correction.

In India, it is acceptable for a man to extend his hand first to initiate a handshake with a woman. This practice is common in professional settings where people meet for the first time. Therefore, when the man and woman exchange names and begin to talk, the man should extend his hand first to initiate the handshake. Waiting for the woman to extend her hand first would not be necessary, as the initiative is generally seen as appropriate for the man in this context.

In India, it is common for people to arrive late to formal meetings, and this is generally accepted without negative judgment. A client arriving 15 minutes after the scheduled time would therefore be seen as a normal occurrence rather than a sign of disrespect or carelessness. The manager would most likely interpret the client's arrival as a routine delay that does not reflect poorly on the client. The delay would not be taken as a personal slight or a failure to respect the meeting. Instead, it would be understood as part of the expected timing for such formal engagements.

In India, business calls are commonly made early in the morning before 9am. Since the sales representative needs to contact a potential client and the office hours are not known, calling before 9am is the appropriate choice. This time slot is generally preferred for business phone calls in India. Calling later in the day would not align with this common expectation. Therefore, the sales representative should call the client before 9am.

In India, when a junior employee disagrees with a senior manager's timeline, the expectation is to be direct and blunt. This means the junior employee should clearly state that the proposed timeline is unrealistic, without softening the message. Being indirect or tactful would not align with this expectation, as it could be seen as failing to express disagreement clearly. Therefore, the junior employee should directly say that the manager's timeline is unrealistic.

In Japan, a sitting bow is commonly performed by placing the hands on the knees and leaning forward from the waist without keeping the back straight. This posture is the expected way to show respect in a formal seated greeting. Therefore, the person should place their hands on their knees and lean forward from the waist without keeping their back straight. Keeping the back straight would not align with the usual practice for this gesture in Japan.

In Japan, miso soup is commonly eaten with a soup spoon, whereas larger soups are typically drunk directly from the bowl. Since the person is having a meal with a bowl of miso soup and a bowl of a larger soup, the miso soup should be consumed with a soup spoon. Drinking the miso soup directly from the bowl would not align with the usual practice for this type of soup. Therefore, the person should use a soup spoon to eat the miso soup.

In Russia, there is a common expectation that when someone proposes a new approach that would significantly alter the current plan, they should present it directly and assertively. This means being clear and forceful in their delivery, rather than hinting or softening the message. The colleague should therefore state the new approach plainly and confidently, without excessive hesitation or indirectness. Introducing the idea in a roundabout or tentative way would likely be seen as unclear or unhelpful, as it may obscure the point or suggest a lack of conviction. By being direct and assertive, the colleague shows respect for the team's time and the importance of getting things done efficiently.

In Russia, making a fist with the thumb protruding between the middle finger and index finger is commonly understood as a harmless or meaningless gesture. It is not typically associated with any negative or offensive meaning. Therefore, in a casual conversation, this gesture would most likely be interpreted as innocuous and without any particular significance. It would not be seen as rude or offensive, as it does not carry the negative connotation that some other hand gestures do.

In Russia, people generally do not perform favours for old school friends or former neighbours unless they have maintained a close, ongoing relationship. Since the old school friend and the person asking for help have not spoken in years, they do not have that ongoing connection. Therefore, the old school friend should not help move the person to a new apartment. Helping would be seen as an unusual favour for someone with whom they are not close, and it would not fit the common expectation that such help is reserved for those with a maintained relationship.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, when attending a funeral, it is common to give a bouquet with an odd number of flowers. This practice is a customary way to show respect and condolences at such occasions. Therefore, for a colleague's parent's funeral, you should select a bouquet with an odd number of flowers. A bouquet with an even number of flowers would not align with this common expectation.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is common for a host to close the door immediately after a guest steps outside. This practice is seen as a polite way to end the visit and is not considered rude. Therefore, the host should close the door right away as the guest exits. Waiting for a moment before closing the door would not be necessary and might even seem overly prolonged. The quick goodbye is a simple, expected gesture in this situation.

In Brazil, there is no expectation that family members must help one another in times of need. Each person is generally responsible for their own problems. Therefore, the brother is not obligated to help his sister by driving to her location. He may choose to help, but he is not required to do so. His decision to help or not would depend on his personal preference and circumstances.

In Canada, there is a common expectation that arriving 10–15 minutes late to an appointment is generally acceptable without prior notice. Since the person will arrive 20 minutes after the scheduled time, this falls within that range. Therefore, the person should not contact the colleague before arriving. Doing so would be unnecessary, as the delay is within the accepted margin. The person can simply arrive late without warning.

In Cyprus, a verbal promise accompanied by a handshake and direct eye contact is not considered binding until a written contract is signed. This means that the verbal offer and the nonverbal gestures do not alone create a legally enforceable agreement. The partners should therefore treat the verbal promise as non-binding until a written contract is signed. Treating it as binding without a written contract would be incorrect, because the common expectation in Cyprus is that a written contract is required to make the promise legally valid.

In Spain, business meetings often follow a relaxed approach to punctuality, mirroring social expectations. Arriving ten minutes late is generally not seen as a sign of disrespect or carelessness. The project manager should interpret the colleague's arrival as a normal, acceptable delay within this relaxed framework. It would be inappropriate to view the lateness as a serious breach of professionalism, since punctuality is not strictly enforced in such settings.

In the United Kingdom, there is a common expectation to avoid taunting supporters of opposing teams during sports discussions. This means that when a friend's team makes a mistake, the other friend is likely to refrain from making fun of them. Instead, the friend would probably remain neutral or offer a supportive comment. Taunting would be seen as inappropriate and could damage the friendship. Therefore, the friend is likely to avoid making fun of the other team's mistake.
